A cyberattack disrupted operations at B2B top-up solutions provider GlobeTopper, causing an estimated $2.5 million in lost revenue, while the attacker redeemed digital gift cards worth $70,000.
Parent company iQSTEL said that the intrusion was detected on October 22 and GlobeTopper responded by suspending its platform and starting an investigation.
GlobeTopper is a business-to-business digital gift card distributor. Various retailers, fintech apps, and rewards platforms use its API. According to the platform’s website, it is used by more than 4,000 brands across 65 countries, including IKEA, Adidas, Spotify, Target, and Roblox.
In a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), iQSTEL said that GlobeTopper detected more unauthorized activity the day after it identified the attack. In response, the company "took the platform and all affected servers offline" in the early hours of October 23 to investigate and fix the problem.
The company deployed a completely rebuilt platform on AWS on October 31, while commercial operations were restored in stages, starting November 1.
GlobeTopper says the attacker obtained certain client API credentials and integration keys, which have been revoked and replaced, and it has observed no unauthorized use of them yet.
“During its investigation, the Company determined that the unauthorized party obtained API credentials and integration keys of certain GlobeTopper business customers,” iQSTEL says.
“All affected credentials and integration keys have been revoked and rotated, and affected business customers have been issued new credentials subject to additional access restrictions.”
The company further stated that an investigation is ongoing to determine whether other customer, personal, payment, or provider data was accessed or acquired.
Regarding the digital gift cards the attackers redeemed, the company says it cannot block, recover, or reclaim them, and will incur the losses.
iQSTEL said the incident hurt GlobeTopper’s fourth-quarter transaction volume and operating results, but as of the filing, it has not determined it to be material.
BleepingComputer has emailed iQSTEL with additional questions regarding the incident, but the company declined to share further information.
At the time of writing, no ransomware groups have listed iQSTEL or GlobeTopper as victims on their extortion portals.

content:
香港政府在大埔火灾一周年之前宣布，不会举办任何官方纪念活动，同时公布了针对悲剧受害者的新补贴计划。 2025年12月10日，一束鲜花被留在大埔宏福苑附近的路边。2025年11月26日，一场致命大火，吞没了该住宅区八个街区中的七个。照片：何凯莉/HKFP。政务司司长陈家伟周二在商业电台表示，当局不会举办任何活动悼念火灾遇难者，因为社区已经开展了各种活动，包括宗教团体组织的活动。陈补充说，政府不会阻碍合法的纪念活动，并且在某些情况下会提供安排交通等协助。不过，陈敦促公众“谨慎”选择纪念活动，并指出网上有些人试图利用纪念活动“制造麻烦”。陈的这番言论是在 11 月 26 日大埔火灾一周年纪念日之前发表的。一些纪念活动的组织者似乎面临着当局的压力，一些教堂收到了警方的询问，活动突然被取消。与此同时，政府宣布为火灾受害者提供两项新的补助金，总额约为6.3亿港元，帮助他们“尽快开始新的生活”。民政及青年事务局局长麦惠文会见传媒。
民政及青年事务局局长麦家丽周二向传媒表示，在“新起点支援津贴”计划下，每间单位的业主将获发30万港元的补助金，而每名死者家属将获发20万港元的补助金。这些补助金将从宏福苑支援基金中拨出，该基金是一项政府主导的基金，已向企业和公众筹集了 45 亿港元。麦说，火灾发生一年后，支持基金“已基本用完”。该基金约28亿港元已指定用于支持政府买断受火灾影响的宏福苑住宅小区的所有物业。 “化悲痛为动力” 去年11月26日，大埔宏福苑住宅小区发生火灾。当该庄园正在进行大规模翻修工程时，它从一栋建筑开始，迅速蔓延到其他六个街区。这是该市几十年来最严重的火灾，夺去了 168 人的生命，其中包括 10 名家庭佣工，并导致数千人无家可归。调查这起致命火灾的独立委员会一个月前向政府提交了一份关于火灾原因和建议的报告。行政长官李家超在10月下旬的新闻发布会上带领高层官员宣布时任房屋署署长何温妮因火灾辞职，并根据委员会的建议采取了一系列改革措施。
布政司陈家祥。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。陈表示，政府将全面落实火灾后成立的独立委员会提出的全部 120 项建议。他补充说，其中近 30 项建议已经推出，其余近 90% 的建议要么已准备好实施，要么已经在实施中，其中绝大多数将于明年完成。 “我也是一名香港人。这起事件是如此严重、令人心碎和悲伤……现在已经一年多了

【原文 English Original】
The Hong Kong government has announced ahead of the first anniversary of the fatal Tai Po fire that it will not host any official memorial activities, while unveiling new subsidy schemes for victims of the tragedy. A bouquet of flowers is left on a roadside near Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po, on December 10, 2025. A deadly blaze broke out on November 26, 2025, and engulfed seven of the eight blocks of the housing estate. Photo: Kelly Ho/HKFP. Chief Secretary for Administration Eric Chan said on Commercial Radio on Tuesday that authorities would not host any events to mourn the fire victims, as various activities, including those organised by religious groups, were already underway in the community. Chan added that the government would not obstruct legal memorial activities and would, in some cases, offer assistance such as arranging transportation. However, Chan urged the public to choose memorial activities “carefully,” noting that some people online were attempting to use memorial events to “make trouble.” Chan’s remarks came ahead of the first anniversary of the Tai Po fire on November 26. Organisers of some memorial activities have appeared to face pressure from authorities, with some churches receiving police enquiries and an event abruptly cancelled . Meanwhile, the government announced two new grants for the fire victims, totalling around HK$630 million, to help them “start a new life as soon as possible.” Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak meets the press. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak told the press on Tuesday that under the “New Beginning Support Grants” scheme, the owner of each flat would be offered HK$300,000, while another grant of HK$200,000 would be provided to the family of each deceased victim. The grants will be disbursed from the Support Fund for Wang Fuk Court, a government-led fund that has raised HK$4.5 billion from corporations and members of the public. Mak said that one year after the fire, the support fund “has been largely used up.” About HK$2.8 billion from the fund has been earmarked to support the government’s buyout of all property titles at the fire-hit Wang Fuk Court residential estate. ‘Channel sorrow into motivation’ On November 26 last year, a blaze broke out at the Wang Fuk Court residential estate in Tai Po. It started in one building and quickly spread to six other blocks while the estate was undergoing a large-scale renovation project. It was the deadliest blaze the city had seen in decades, claiming 168 lives, including 10 domestic workers, and leaving thousands homeless. An independent committee probing the deadly fire submitted a report on its causes and recommendations to the government a month ago. Chief Executive John Lee led top officials at a press conference in late October to announce that then-housing chief Winnie Ho had resigned over the blaze , alongside a series of reform measures based on the committee’s recommendations. Chief Secretary Eric Chan. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Chan said the government would fully implement all 120 recommendations put forward by the independent committee established following the fire. Nearly 30 of the recommendations have already been rolled out, while nearly 90 per cent of the remainder are either ready for implementation or already underway, with the vast majority set to be completed next year, he added. “I am also a Hongkonger. This incident was so severe, heartbreaking and sad… It has now been a year and our hearts are heavy. But from the perspective of the government, we should channel our sorrow into motivation for transformation, and make sure there will not be another such incident in the future,” Chan said in Cantonese.

title: Beijing hails ‘healthy competition’ after small-circle vote for body that selects Hong Kong’s leader
zh_title: 在小圈子投票选出香港领导人后，北京赞扬“良性竞争”
summary: 北京负责香港事务的最高机构对周日小圈选举委员会竞选的投票率创历史新高表示欢迎，一些重量级候选人意外落选。 2026年11月22日，选举管理委员会主席乐大卫（右二）与政制及内地事务局局长谢淑丽（左二）在香港会议展览中心举行的2026年选举委员会界别分组一般选举中央点票站清空投票箱。图片：香港政府一站通。国家港澳事务办公室
content:
北京负责香港事务的最高机构对周日小圈选举委员会竞选的投票率创历史新高表示欢迎，一些重量级候选人意外落选。 2026年11月22日，选举管理委员会主席乐大卫（右二）与政制及内地事务局局长谢淑丽（左二）在香港会议展览中心举行的2026年选举委员会界别分组一般选举中央点票站清空投票箱。图片：香港政府一站通。中国国务院港澳事务办公室周一表示，组建负责选举香港领导人的强大选举委员会的竞争体现了“良性竞争”。只有一小部分香港人口有资格在周日的选举中投票，5,709 名符合资格的选民中有 5,640 人参加了投票，投票率达到创纪录的 98.8%。整个香港约有410万登记选民。周日共有 856 名候选人角逐 31 个界别分组的 723 个议席。另外 259 个席位没有竞争，其中 362 个席位由当然成员填补，156 个席位由指定机构的代表填补。他们将共同组成由 1,500 人组成的选举委员会，该委员会将在明年的行政长官选举中进行提名和投票。它还将在2029年的下一次立法会选举中提名和选举90名立法会议员中的40名。
港澳事务办公室发言人周一在一份中文声明中表示，“这次选举委员会竞选再次体现了新选举制度的广泛代表性、政治包容性、均衡参与性、公平竞争性。”该发言人表示，“这次选举真正实现了‘选贤任能’的目标。”选举管理委员会主席乐大卫（中）于2026年11月22日在选举事务处首席选举主任（策划及研究）赵博恩（右）陪同下参观位于港湾道体育馆的2026年选举委员会界别分组一般选举投票站，了解选举活动的情况。图片：香港政府一站通。自北京于2021年彻底改革香港选举制度以确保只有“爱国者”治理香港以来，周日的选举是强大的选举委员会的第二次选举。 2021年3月，北京通过立法，确保“爱国者”治理香港。此举减少了立法机构中的民主代表性，加强了对选举的控制，并引入了一个亲北京的审查小组来选择候选人。当局表示，此次整顿确保了这座城市的稳定和繁荣。但这些变化也引发了国际社会的谴责，因为许多传统反对派仍然身陷囹圄、自我流放或退出政坛。
解说：北京的选举改革 解说：新的选举规则 但周日的竞选也给一些政治重量级人物带来了意外的损失。令人意外的是，香港律师会会长汤智恩未能在 15 名议员的法律界界别分组中获得席位，而香港总商会首席执行官杨伟雄也在 17 名商业（第一）界别分组的竞标中落败。周日，多名富豪和商界领袖当选，其中包括盈科拓展集团主席李泽楷、香港首富李嘉诚的小儿子和信和集团董事长。

【原文 English Original】
Beijing’s top body overseeing Hong Kong affairs has hailed the record turnout in Sunday’s small-circle Election Committee race, which saw some heavyweight candidates suffer surprise losses. Electoral Affairs Commission (EAC) chair David Lok (second right), and the Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs, Janice Tse (second left), empty a ballot box at the Central Counting Station of the 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections located at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre on November 22, 2026. Photo: GovHK. The Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office of the State Council, China’s cabinet, said on Monday that the race to form the powerful Election Committee tasked with choosing the city’s leader embodied “healthy competition.” Only a tiny fraction of Hong Kong’s population was eligible to vote in Sunday’s race, in which 5,640 of 5,709 eligible electors cast ballots — a record-breaking 98.8 per cent turnout. Hong Kong as a whole has about 4.1 million registered voters. A total of 856 candidates were vying for 723 seats across 31 subsectors on Sunday. A further 259 seats were uncontested while 362 were filled by ex-officio members and 156 by representatives of designated bodies. Together they will form the 1,500-strong Election Committee, which will nominate and vote in next year’s chief executive election. It will also nominate and elect 40 of the 90 lawmakers in the next Legislative Council election in 2029. “This Election Committee race once again demonstrates the broad representativeness, political inclusiveness, balanced participation, and fair competition of the new electoral system,” a spokesperson for the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office said in a Chinese-language statement on Monday. “This race truly achieves the goal of ‘selecting the virtuous and capable,'” the spokesperson said. Electoral Affairs Commission chair David Lok (centre), accompanied by the Principal Electoral Officer (Planning and Research) of the Registration and Electoral Office, Brian Chiu (right), visits the polling station of the 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections located at Harbour Road Sports Centre to observe how electoral activities are conducted on November 22, 2026. Photo: GovHK. Sunday’s race was the second for the powerful Election Committee since Beijing overhauled Hong Kong’s electoral system in 2021 to ensure only “patriots” govern the city. In March 2021, Beijing passed legislation to ensure “patriots” govern Hong Kong . The move reduced democratic representation in the legislature, tightened control of elections and introduced a pro-Beijing vetting panel to select candidates. Authorities say the overhaul ensures the city’s stability and prosperity . But the changes also prompted international condemnation , as much of the traditional opposition remains behind bars , in self-exile or has quit politics. Explainer: Beijing’s electoral overhaul Explainer: New electoral rules But Sunday’s race also returned unexpected losses for some political heavyweights. In a surprise upset, Law Society of Hong Kong president Roden Tong failed to secure a seat in the 15-member legal subsector, while Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce CEO Patrick Yeung also fell short in his bid for the 17-strong commercial (first) subsector. Multiple tycoons and business leaders were elected on Sunday, including Pacific Century Group chair Richard Li, the younger son of Hong Kong’s wealthiest person, Li Ka-shing, and Sino Group chair Daryl Ng.

zh_title: 海军陆战队侦察兵参加芬兰海军演习和波罗的海北约海军演习
summary: 2026 年 11 月 7 日，美国海军陆战队部队侦察连、第 2 侦察营、第 2 海军陆战师在芬兰南部海岸的北约增强警戒活动波罗的海哨兵期间进行船只行动。美国海军陆战队照片 作为芬兰海军演习和北约增强警戒活动 (eVA) 波罗的海哨兵的一部分，四打海军陆战队侦察兵本周将在芬兰执行任务。芬兰海军的窄水域 26-2 演习将于周三在芬兰南部沿海地区和芬兰湾开始。此次演习将持续到12月。 4. 练习是
content:
2026 年 11 月 7 日，美国海军陆战队部队侦察连、第 2 侦察营、第 2 海军陆战师在芬兰南部海岸的北约增强警戒活动波罗的海哨兵期间进行船只行动。美国海军陆战队照片 作为芬兰海军演习和北约增强警戒活动 (eVA) 波罗的海哨兵的一部分，四打海军陆战队侦察兵本周将在芬兰执行任务。芬兰海军的窄水域 26-2 演习将于周三在芬兰南部沿海地区和芬兰湾开始。此次演习将持续到12月。 4. 此次演习是芬兰海军秋季的主要演习，芬兰海军舰艇和部队与北约盟国在波罗的海北部及其沿岸进行联合海军作战训练。据芬兰海军新闻稿称，除了芬兰人员、船只和飞机外，爱沙尼亚海军指挥和支援舰EML Wambola (A433)以及约50名美国海军陆战队人员也将参加此次演习。这支海军陆战队共有四​​打成员，来自海军陆战队第二师第二侦察营和驻扎在北卡罗来纳州勒琼海军陆战队基地的第二海军陆战队远征军信息大队。该大队于 10 月初在欧洲海军陆战队轮调部队 (MRF-E) 的指挥下进行前沿部署，当时他们的任务是向芬兰提供先进的远征监视和战术侦察能力，同时与波罗的海哨兵指挥下的终点海岸旅一起作战。
该部队部署的能力包括 Stalker VXE-30 无人机系统 (UAS)。芬兰国防军和边防部队的约 3,500 名人员，包括应征入伍者和预备役军人，正在参加“狭窄水域 26-2”行动。新闻稿中写道：“这次演习是测试 12 月份应征入伍的部队组成技能的机会，也是训练预备役人员执行战时任务的机会。”芬兰陆军和芬兰空军将在南海岸和波罗的海北部利用直升机、战斗机和无人系统进行与演习相关的飞行活动。美国海军陆战队参谋中士。巴尼·南 (Barney South) 是海军陆战队第二师第二侦察营第二部队侦察连的一名海军陆战队队员，在 2026 年 5 月 22 日于芬兰穆斯塔马举行的狭窄水域 26 演习中，在两栖插入期间占据安全位置。 美国海军陆战队照片 芬兰海军还将利用这次演习让芬兰公司测试新技术，包括各种无人系统以及监视和保护设备。海军操作环境。该军种将收集演习的反馈，用它来评估测试系统对海军防御的贡献。演习结束后，美国海军陆战队将恢复参加自10月以来一直在进行的波罗的海哨兵活动。
北约于 2025 年 1 月启动了波罗的海哨兵，以阻止进一步破坏波罗的海关键水下基础设施的企图。根据美国海军陆战队在北约演习中发布的信息，在 10 月份的波罗的海哨兵期间，美国海军陆战队与芬兰部队合作提供远征监视和战术侦察能力，加强海域意识并支持保护重要海底基础设施的努力。 “这一努力展示了海军陆战队远征能力如何补充盟军海上力量、提高信息能力

【原文 English Original】
U.S. Marines with Force Reconnaissance Company, 2d Reconnaissance Battalion, 2d Marine Division, conduct boat operations during NATO Enhanced Vigilance Activity Baltic Sentry off the coast of southern Finland, Nov. 7, 2026. US Marine Corps photo Four dozen Reconnaissance Marines will operate in Finland this week as part of a Finnish naval exercise and NATO’s enhanced Vigilant Activity (eVA) Baltic Sentry. The Finnish Navy’s Narrow Waters 26-2 drill will begin Wednesday in the coastal areas of Southern Finland and in the Gulf of Finland. The exercise will run throughDec. 4. The exercise is the Finnish Navy’s main exercise in autumn and involves Finnish Navy ships and troops and NATO allies training in combined naval operations in the northern Baltic Sea and its coast. In addition to Finnish personnel, ships and aircraft, Estonian Navy command and support ship EML Wambola (A433) and about 50 U.S. Marine Corps personnel will participate in the exercise, according to a Finnish Navy news release . The Marine force –four dozen members – are from 2nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 2nd Marine Division and II Marine Expeditionary Force Information Group based out of Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune, N.C. The group were forward deployed in early October under Marine Rotational Force-Europe (MRF-E) when they were tasked to Finland to provide advanced expeditionary surveillance and tactical reconnaissance capabilities while operating alongside the Finish Coastal Brigade under Baltic Sentry. The capabilities fielded by the unit include the Stalker VXE-30 Unmanned Aerial System (UAS). Approximately 3,500 personnel, including conscripts and reservists, of the Finnish Defense Forces and Border Guard are participating in Narrow Waters 26-2. “The exercise is an opportunity to test the skills of conscripts mustering out in December in their unit compositions, and train reservists for their wartime tasks,” reads the release. The Finnish Army and Finnish Air Force will conduct exercise-related flight activity with helicopters, fighters and unmanned systems on the south coast and northern Baltic Sea. U.S. Marine Corps Staff Sgt. Barney South, a force reconnaissance Marine with 2nd Force Reconnaissance Company, 2nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 2nd Marine Division, holds a security position during an amphibious insertion as part of exercise Narrow Waters 26 in Mustamaa, Finland, May 22, 2026. US Marine Corps photo The Finnish Navy will also use the exercise to have Finnish companies test new technology, including various unmanned systems and surveillance and protection equipment, in a naval operating environment. The service will collect feedback from the exercise, using it to assess the contribution of the tested systems to naval defense. Following completion of the exercise, the U.S. Marines will resume their participation in Baltic Sentry activities, which has been ongoing since October. NATO launched Baltic Sentry in January of 2025 to deter further attempts to damage critical underwater infrastructure in the Baltic Sea. During Baltic Sentry in October, U.S. Marines worked alongside Finnish forces to provide expeditionary surveillance and tactical reconnaissance capabilities, strengthening maritime domain awareness and supporting efforts to protect critical undersea infrastructure, according to a U.S. Marine Corps release on the NATO exercise. “The effort demonstrated how Marine Corps expeditionary capabilities can complement Allied maritime forces, improve information sharing, and contribute to security across the Baltic maritime environment,” reads the release. U.S. Marine Corps Major General Daniel Shipley, Commander, U.S. Marine Corps Forces Europe and Africa, met with Rear Admiral Tuomas Tiilikainen, Commander of the Finnish Navy on Nov. 6 in Finland to discuss NATO interoperability, the U.S.-Finnish defense relationship and the role of combined forces in defending the Alliance’s northern and eastern flanks, according to the release. The engagement highlighted the ongoing partnership between the U.S. Marine Corps and Finnish Navy and the importance of integrating capabilities within a broader Nordic force prepared to defend NATO territory, reads the release. U.S. Marines with 2nd Force Reconnaissance Company, 2nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 2nd Marine Division, board a U-600 Jurmo LCP Watercat M12 during Finnish weapons and boat familiarization training as part of exercise Narrow Waters 26 in Upinniemi, Finland, May 15, 2026. US Marine Corps photo In Narrow Waters 26.2, Finnish, Estonian and U.S. forces will train together to refine maritime command and control, reconnaissance, fire coordination and Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) defense. The exercise is meant to strengthen participants’ ability to share information, synchronize operations and integrate complementary capabilities in a complex maritime environment, reads the release. “When Allies train together in demanding environments, we build the trust, capability, and combat credibility required to operate as one combined force,” said Shipley in the release. “Our Finnish allies are highly capable. The [U.S] Marines are here to sharpen interoperability with Finnish and Estonian allies, strengthen maritime readiness, and ensure our Alliance remains prepared to meet any challenge.” Finnish, Estonian and U.S. personnel will train at the task group, task unit and unit levels to strengthen coordination and improve their ability to operate together. The Recon Marines will contribute reconnaissance, fires liaison and coordination, command and control, and CBRN defense capabilities. “These contributions will help participating forces strengthen maritime domain awareness, integrate air and missile defense, coordinate strike capabilities, and rehearse responses to CBRN threats,” reads the release. As part of its transition to Force Design 2030, the Marine Corps has not only been carrying out training in distributed and dispersed operations in the Indo-Pacific but also in Northern Europe. Along with participation in Baltic Sentry, the service deployed expeditionary long-range missile systems to Norway in August and September under Operation Atlantic City 26 . The Marine Corps also continues to carry out conventional warfare training in Norway with 3,000 Marines deploying to Norway in March for exercise Cold Response .

互动：跟踪 COP31 气候峰会上的谈判文本 互动：在 COP31 气候变化峰会上谁想要什么 由于严重分歧阻碍了就主席主导的协议达成一致，《联合国气候变化框架公约》主席西蒙·斯蒂尔表示“深感失望”，他谈到了联合国气候进程的“改进、现代化和改革的空间”。闭幕全体会议。其中包括为全球“公正转型”建立新“机制”的相当有限的或程序性的成果，以及对遭受气候灾难的国家的支持。不过，谈判之外还取得了一些进展，越来越多的国家联盟倡导“摆脱”化石燃料的“路线图”。随着主席国推动“电气化”成为关键主题，约 80 个国家还签署了到 2035 年确保 35% 的最终能源消耗来自电力的全球目标。在此，Carbon Brief 深入分析了安塔利亚会议在 COP31 谈判内外的所有关键成果。

Print article Share Article Contents Expand menu Close Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Cover decision COP reform Adaptation Finance Just transition work programme Loss and damage Gender Article 6 Agriculture and food security Mitigation work programme Response measures Action for climate empowerment Trade Second global stocktake Long-term goal review Around the COP Fossil fuels Action agenda Global leaders Electrification China at COP31 Ocean Deforestation Methane New climate science Food and water NDCs Protests and access Road to COP32 and beyond The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, have failed to reach agreement on a “pact” that lacked clear references to curbing fossil fuels or scaling up climate finance . The “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, was rejected in the final hours by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations. Meanwhile, many developing countries criticised the lack of progress on climate finance and indecision on a proposed $120bn target for funding climate adaptation. COP31 coverage COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31 Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31? Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’? Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit With stark divisions preventing agreement on the presidency-led pact, UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell expressed “deep disappointment”, speaking of “scope to improve, modernise and reform” the UN climate process. Despite a chaotic endgame that saw the overrunning COP become the longest in history, it did not end in complete failure, with many items adopted in the closing plenary. These included fairly limited or procedural outcomes on a new “ mechanism ” for global “ just transitions ”, plus support for countries struck by climate disasters. There was some progress beyond the negotiations, though, with growing coalitions of nations championing “ roadmaps ” for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels. With the presidency promoting “ electrification ” as a key theme, around 80 nations also signed up to a global target of securing 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Here, Carbon Brief provides in-depth analysis of all the key outcomes from Antalya, both inside and outside the COP31 negotiations. (See Carbon Brief’s coverage of COP30 , COP29 , COP28 , COP27 , COP26 , COP25 , COP24 , COP23 , COP22 , COP21 and COP20 .) Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Cover decision COP reform Adaptation Finance Just transition work programme Loss and damage Gender Article 6 Agriculture and food security Mitigation work programme Response measures Action for climate empowerment Trade Second global stocktake Long-term goal review Guidance on NDCs Rio synergies Around the COP Fossil fuels Action agenda Global leaders Electrification China at COP31 Ocean Deforestation Methane New climate science Food and water NDCs Protests and access Road to COP32 and beyond Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Turkey and Australia presided over the longest COP in history – and failed to find consensus on their proposed “cover decision”, exposing deep fractures between countries on key issues such as fossil fuels and the need for developed nations to meet climate-finance pledges. Experts told Carbon Brief that, strictly, the talks did not “collapse” as several negotiated items were still adopted. Rather, the rejection of the cover decision represented, for the first time, “those who want a higher level of ambition actively reject[ing] the lowest common denominator on offer”, said one veteran observer. Dispute over who would host COP31 – representing the “western Europe and other states” region – had gone on for three years . In the end, the two main rivals, Turkey and Australia, agreed to a deal last year at COP30 that the summit would take place in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia acting as “president of negotiations”. COP31 president and Turkish minister Murat Kurum and COP31 “president of negotiations” and Australian minister Chris Bowen. Credit: ENB Critics questioned whether either country was well-placed to host, given their ongoing fossil-fuel expansion. Turkey faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of the summit, while recent Carbon Brief analysis found that Australia is the third-largest CO2 exporter in history because of its fossil-fuel production. Ahead of the summit, the presidency released four official letters outlining a vision for COP31. The first letter , written by COP31 president Murat Kurum in April 2026, confirmed the appointment of Australian climate minister Chris Bowen as “president of the negotiations” and announced that a pre-COP would be held in Fiji in October. The second letter , authored by both Kurum and Bowen from the Copenhagen climate ministerial in May, said that “COP31 presents a vital opportunity to further accelerate…in the areas of clean energy, electrification and resilient infrastructure”. The third letter , published in August 2026, gave more details on the presidency’s plans for the “ action agenda ” – the part of the UN process that mobilises coalitions of nations and non-state actors to push climate action further. This letter also introduced a key aim from the presidency to get countries to agree to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 (often referred to as “35 by 35”). (See: Electrification .) The final letter , published in October ahead of the pre-COP in Fiji, said that the presidency would centre on “delivering a COP focused on accelerating implementation, electrification and resilience in an uncertain world”. It added that “many parties have emphasised the importance of reviewing and continuously improving UNFCCC processes, to ensure it remains fit for purpose, sustainable and focused as negotiations evolve over time”, adding: “At COP31, we will hold presidency consultations to hear parties’ views on how to strengthen UNFCCC processes, to ensure growing demands are met and to effectively deploy resources.” The pre-COP in Fiji was held from 5-8 October and was attended by 3,000 people. In this somewhat intimate setting, Bowen announced that Turkey and Australia had agreed to negotiate a “presidency-led” cover decision at COP31. He added that revealing this before COP was part of the presidency’s “upfront, transparent and consultative approach”. Later that month, the presidency named the five ministerial pairs from developed and developing countries that would take key negotiation issues forward at COP31. These issues were mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and oceans. COP31 kicked off on 9 November, with climate negotiations scholar (and Carbon Brief contributing editor ) Dr Joanna Depledge noting that it was clear from the summit’s opening ceremony that “Australia [was] the junior partner” in the presidency. COP’s opening day ran late into the night as the presidency worked to avert a fight over proposed changes to the summit’s negotiations agenda. Simon Evans 9 November 2026, 10:40 GMT COP31: Agenda adopted! Agenda adopted! Moments ago in Antalya, Turkey, COP31 president Murat Kurum outlined how an “agenda fight” has been averted, despite various proposals for additions to proceedings. This came after a short delay, while a series of huddles took place on… Read more on CB Connect → The next day, in plenary, Kurum announced that a resolution had been found. He said that calls for new agenda items on adaptation finance and trade were rejected, whereas an item on a new climate finance “work programme” had been added. (The EU expressed “deep concern” about the addition.) Kurum added that two extra proposed items on mountains and climate change – made more poignant by recent catastrophic floods in Nepal – were also not added to the agenda. However, he said that the presidency would instead hold consultations on the topic. Though an early scrap over the agenda was avoided, the summit’s opening days were plagued with logistical problems. Attendees were forced to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to get into the venue – sparking serious access concerns . People queuing to enter the COP31 venue in Antalya, Turkey. Credit: ZUMA Press, Inc. / Alamy Stock Photo The problems persisted into the first day of the world leaders’ summit on 11 November, when delegates were informed that they should travel between the hours of 5-7am to secure access to the venue. Ire only grew when security staff still let people in after this time. On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This was an “informal note” with a bullet-pointed list of topics that might be included. On Saturday evening, Kurum told a press conference that “around 30 countries” had indicated support for the 35 by 35 pledge. However, he had little to share on progress in the negotiations and eluded questions on how he planned to include “fossil fuels” in the cover decision. In the small hours of Sunday morning, half-way through the summit, Kurum announced presidency and ministerial consultations on “outstanding political issues”. He also invited ministers to a “divan” – a group meeting, not a daybed – to discuss cross-cutting issues. On Monday afternoon, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “ presidency note ” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text. (See: Cover decision .) At a press conference, Bowen told journalists that the presidency decided to release the text “early” to allow parties to debate on it for as long as possible and acknowledged that it would need to be “refined” down. On Wednesday evening, the presidency held its divan, where delegation heads sat in a circle and were asked to share their priorities for finding consensus in the negotiations. Countries take part in a “divan” at COP31. Credit: UNFCCC / Flickr Speaking at the divan, Kurum told parties that the second draft cover decision would be published that evening. In the end, the second draft cover decision was published on Thursday. Later that day, Kurum and Bowen spoke at a press conference, talking up their latest draft with lofty claims that it could “achieve [the] covenant of 1.5C and nothing more”. However, the second draft was rejected by countries and civil society alike. (See: Cover decision .) On Friday – the summit’s last scheduled day – the mood at COP soured. With few official updates, delegates relied on ever-changing rumours about when a new text might emerge. Negotiations on other key issues also remained stuck, as civil society dubbed it the “worst COP in history” at a press conference attended by Carbon Brief.  In the evening, the presidency opened the closing plenary to gavel through non-contentious items – and announced that a new text would not be released until Saturday morning.  They were interrupted by a protester wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” and with a red noose around their neck. As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update failed to arrive.  An open letter signed by 100 civil society organisations told the presidency it was “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had”. As Turkish support staff started packing down the party pavilions, behind-the-scenes disputes between country ministers intensified. Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UK, the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean (AILAC), the Umbrella Group (UG) and least-developed countries (LDCs) – approached the presidency as a united front to demand changes to the cover decision. These changes included on how it referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, adaptation finance and carbon capture and storage. width: 64px; align-self: start; } } Membership Support award-winning climate journalism Join CB+ A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.  With official updates still few and far between, rumours swirled that many countries were still not happy with this iteration of the text and planned to reject it. Later that day, another version of the text arrived – but it contained only minor changes. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, several countries rejected the cover decision – citing reasons including its failure to respond to humanity’s overshoot of 1.5C of global warming, its failure to clearly mention fossil fuels and its lack of clear figures for adaptation finance. (See: Cover decision .) While countries rejected the cover decision, they did find consensus on other texts, including for the just transition work programme , the global goal on adaptation , the climate finance work programme , carbon markets , long-term finance and “Article 2.1c”. The final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time – nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end. This makes COP31 the longest in history.  Cover decision The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 counties during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious –  closing plenary in Antalya. Towards the end of the summit, Kurum had told a press conference attended by Carbon Brief that he wanted the cover decision to be known as the “Antalya accord”. (This was later amended in the last formal draft to be the “Antalya pact”.) But, in the closing plenary, the EU told the assembled delegates: “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” According to Carbon Brief’s tally during the closing plenary, the agreement was also explicitly rejected by Panama, the Marshall Islands, Belize, Norway and Vanuatu. After it was clear that the pact would not be adopted, the 44-member LDCs, the UK, South Korea and Japan all said that consensus had not been reached, a softer form of indicating dissent. The six-member environmental integrity group (EIG) also registered its “concerns” with the text. For months ahead of the summit, the Turkish and Australian presidencies had been talking up the idea of a COP31 cover decision – an overarching political statement. Indeed, Bowen had publicly raised the idea of a COP31 cover decision at last year’s COP30 in Brazil, even before the agreement to act as joint president with Turkey had been finalised. In his opening speech in Antalya, Bowen said that he had agreed with Kurum to take forward a “presidency-initiated, party-driven [cover] decision for COP31”. He had said at a pre-COP in Fiji: “There is a clear expectation that COP31 must respond to the global moment – to send a clear message to accelerate implementation…And to demonstrate our continued commitment to multilateralism, to international cooperation and to the Paris Agreement.” Bowen stressed that this should not lead to a “lengthy political statement”, but that he wanted it to respond to the imminent “ overshoot ” of 1.5C, the “catastrophic impacts” of warming and the “tangible progress” being made in the energy transition. For Turkey, the cover decision became a vehicle to promote what had started out as its voluntary target for electricity to make up 35% of global final energy by 2035. (See: Electrification .)  While early on, Russia publicly challenged the legal basis for a cover decision, given it was not on the official agenda, these procedural objections fell away as the summit continued. Many other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent . Carbon Brief understands that legal advice from the UNFCCC secretariat confirmed the broad authority of the presidency to initiate a cover decision in Antalya. Nevertheless, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations. For the LMDCs, India told the closing plenary: “We are also acutely aware that [the cover decision] has taken away our attention from the mandated items of the agenda, which we had to deliver.” It had quickly become clear that Bowen’s ambitions for a brief cover decision would be in vain, when a lengthy 144-paragraph “ reflections ” text was released on 16 November. Simon Evans 13 November 2026, 05:55 GMT NEW: COP31 cover decision ‘reflections’ text Today, Friday 13 November, the COP31 presidency published a “reflections” text on consultations it has been holding with heads of national delegations on a potential “cover decision”. This is not a fully formed draft text, but instead contains an organised… Read more on CB Connect → This document was a compilation of all the issues that parties had put forward for inclusion, ranging from quantified climate-finance goals through to firm timelines for the next assessment report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Other ideas included that developed countries should reach net-zero emissions by 2030, that certain trade policies should be “phase[d] out” next year and that the largely defunct Kyoto Protocol should be resurrected, with binding carbon targets for developed nations. The text also included the presidencies’ favoured “35 by 35” electrification target , as well as language on the transition away from fossil fuels. (See: Fossil fuels ). A second iteration – in reality, the first fully formed draft cover decision – was published on 19 November, consisting of just 80 paragraphs. This version was immediately criticised for having excised any mention of fossil fuels, as well as deleting the $120bn adaptation-finance target wanted by developing countries. (See: Adaptation .) It retained the “35 by 35” target, but only as one of a menu of options, listed as areas for “global cooperation” to “keep 1.5C within reach”. Paragraph 36 of the second draft cover text. Source: UNFCCC . Controversially, this menu of options – indicated by the wording “inter alia”, meaning “among other things” – also included numerical targets for carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), apparently as “ quid pro quo ” for the quantified electrification target. The same day, in a highly unusual move, Panama issued an open letter stating that it would “formally object” to any decision not meeting demands including a “cap on oil production”. Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro. A third and supposedly “final” version of the cover decision was published at around 3am local time on Sunday 22 November, already deep into overtime at the summit. This still did not make any direct reference to fossil fuels or the $120bn adaptation finance target. It also removed language that had called for the next IPCC reports to be published ahead of the second “global stocktake”. Carbon Brief has seen proposed revisions presented to the presidency by a 126-nation coalition of countries, including the EU, LDCs, AOSIS, AILAC, EIG and Umbrella groups. They asked for the paragraph above – numbered 36 in the second draft and 40 in the third – to be replaced with a direct link to the first global stocktake, which included the transition away from fossil fuels. (They did not suggest an explicit use of the words “fossil fuels”.) The group also wanted the sub-paragraph with numerical targets for CCUS to be deleted. However, a fourth and final version of the “Antalya pact”, published a few hours later, made only minor changes, softening language on CCUS to “increasing” rather than “accelerating”, while also weakening the language around the timeline for the next IPCC reports. On the last scheduled day of negotiations, Bowen had told journalists: “The world is wondering whether multilateralism can deliver. I think it can.” But the presidencies’ efforts to secure a cover decision were, ultimately, unsuccessful. The UK told the closing plenary: “What is before us is not commensurate with the urgency of overshoot, the scale of the climate crisis or the impacts already being felt…It is the lowest common denominator…[rather than presenting] bold collective ambition on climate action.” Not all parties were opposed to the Antalya pact. Ghana, for the African group, said it could support the decision, despite the lack of specificity on topics including adaptation finance and trade measures. Saudi Arabia, for the Arab group, said that they had continued to “engage constructively” on the cover decision, “despite all of the issues that were taken off the table”, including on finance and historical emissions . It also said: “We cannot reconcile a position that stated so publicly that we need to keep 1.5C within reach and, yet, calling CCUS technologies greenwashing.” Russia explained its steadfast opposition to “any wording on fossil fuels” – despite the wording agreed by consensus at COP28. It criticised “slogans” around the use of fossil fuels, arguing that even in 1.5C pathways, there was an ongoing role for oil and gas. While the failure to adopt a cover decision has been widely compared to the collapsed Copenhagen climate talks in 2015, experts told Carbon Brief this comparison was flawed. Nevertheless, they said it could end the recent trend of COPs attempting to secure a cover decision, as well as sparking renewed reflections on how to reform the process. Paul Watkinson , the French chief negotiator at Paris COP21, told Carbon Brief: “This time it is the political bet of the presidency on a cover decision that has not worked…I think this needs a deeper reflection on what we are trying to achieve – there are limits to political signals in a decision – and we ought to think [about] what we can achieve through the COP and how to make it work better.” COP reform As COP31 ended without agreement on the proposed “Antalya pact”, much of the immediate response focused on perceived shortcomings in the UN climate process. In his closing remarks , UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell said there were “lessons that must be learned” for the consensus-driven process: “Clearly, there is also scope to improve, modernise and reform. But not only because of what happened here. But also because we must evolve in this era of implementation.” In fact, one of the COP31 presidency’s stated priorities had been reforming COPs – or what they described as “strengthen[ing] UNFCCC processes”.  COP reform was discussed during the summit, including at a press conference where Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro told journalists: “The COP has become an exercise in futility…192 countries will not agree on every single comma and every single period…especially those countries that produce carbon-based fuels.” In practice, such bombastic statements were far removed from the on-going discussions and country submissions on COP reform , which had already begun in Brazil last year.  These discussions were integrated into the formal negotiations under the heading of “ arrangements for intergovernmental meetings ” (AIM).  At the Bonn climate talks in June, Australia, along with Turkey, offered to conduct informal consultations on increasing UNFCCC “efficiency” at COP31.  The African group asked for legal clarity and cautioned that “efficiency should not be equated with reducing budgets or removing agenda items” necessary to tackle climate change, according to the Earth Negotiations Bulletin .  Early in the talks, the COP31 presidency published a concept note calling for “forward-looking and exploratory” discussions on what a “strong and effective UNFCCC process” could look like. It also initiated “presidency consultations” on the matter, despite the lack of a clear mandate for doing so. In the presidency consultations, responses included multi-year planning, retiring old agenda items and “avoiding unnecessary cover decisions”.  Several countries – including Russia, the African group, AILAC and the LMDCs – questioned the need for separate discussions and whether these were solely for the cover decision, given they were already underway in the AIM negotiations.  Russia said it “did not consent to elevating this discussion to high political level” and that it was unclear “why such a significant amount of negotiating time [was] being devoted” to these roundtables without a clear objective.  Drafts of the presidency’s failed cover decision included “high-level consultations” under COP presidencies on “strengthening the UNFCCC process”. During the final plenary, Peru, for AILAC, called for a “clear rule on votes” and an independent review of the COP process’s efficiency. Peru’s environment director Andrés Martín Garrido Sánchez said: “To negotiate in good faith is not a courtesy; it’s an obligation. It means not using delays as a strategy. It means negotiating text in the room in the view of everyone, with every party being heard before a decision is gavelled. It means not taking issues hostage…We are not proposing matters against the consensus. This way of negotiating is not leading us to where the world needs us to be.”  With the Antalya pact rejected, these discussions will still continue under AIM in Bonn in 2027. .cb-tweet img{ border: solid 1.25px #333333; border-radius: 5px; } @media (max-width:650px){ .cb-tweet{ width:100%; } } Adaptation While efforts to specify that tripling adaptation finance meant $120bn by 2035 failed to make it into any final texts, COP31 did see a breakthrough on channelling carbon-market revenues into the UN adaptation fund . Disagreements over finance dominated negotiations within the “ global goal on adaptation ” (GGA).  This followed a “call for efforts” to triple adaptation finance by 2035, which was agreed last year at COP30. That target was originally proposed by the LDCs as a “tripling of grant-based adaptation finance by 2030 to at least $120bn”.  Last year’s final agreement was considerably weaker and lacked key details – including the baseline for tripling and what kinds of funding would be counted towards it. Ahead of the start of COP31, the African group requested that the tripling goal be added to the agenda, providing a potential space to discuss these outstanding issues. African group request for agenda item on tripling adaptation finance. Source: UNFCCC . This request was rejected . As a result, the question of where the goal should be discussed quickly arose as a fault line. It was debated within the GGA, the climate finance “work programme”, as well as the proposed “cover decision”.  As negotiations got underway, the G77 and China coalition of developing countries argued that adaptation finance should be discussed in the GGA rooms.  The EU, UK, environmental integrity group (EIG), Norway and Canada all wanted adaptation finance discussed under the climate finance work programme. This would place the tripling goal within the broader $300bn target for 2035 – meaning adaptation finance could come from a wide variety of sources, not just developed-country grants, Over the first week of negotiations, two GGA draft texts were released, both of which included specific references to tripling adaptation finance to $120bn per year by 2035.  This would use a baseline of 2025, when the previous target to double adaptation finance to $40bn per year came to an end.  Draft GGA text on 13 November. Source: UNFCCC . Over the second week of COP31, parties continued to disagree over the home and baseline for the tripling target.  The first draft text on the cover decision – reflecting ideas put forward by parties – included relatively ambitious language that tripling finance for adaptation “should reach at least $120bn”. However, the “$120bn” was absent from the next draft and an accompanying GGA text . NGO network Climate Action Network (CAN) reported that France – as co-chair of the ministerial climate-finance negotiations – had proposed a 2019 baseline, which would reduce the tripling target to just $60bn a year by 2035.  For context, the latest UNEP report on adaptation suggests that developing countries will need a total of $305bn every year by 2035 to meet their adaptation needs. Ultimately, neither the GGA, the climate finance work programme nor the failed cover decision specifically contained a baseline or target figure for tripling adaptation finance. Bethan Laughlin , senior policy specialist at ZSL (Zoological Society of London), told Carbon Brief that the failure to agree a baseline does a “colossal amount of damage, because it is a continued betrayal of promises for finance of all types”.  Beyond finance, parties worked to establish an expert taskforce that could refine the set of 59 “indicators” for the global goal on adaptation, which had been agreed at COP30, as part of the two-year “Belém-Addis vision”. These are the metrics that countries will use to assess their progress in adapting to climate change. Speaking to Carbon Brief, Emilie Beauchamp , senior adaptation expert at International Institute for Sustainable Development ( IISD ), highlighted that the indicators had been pushed through in Brazil without full engagement from parties. She added:   “It ties into the bigger picture, which is that [the] Brazilian presidency’s cover decision didn’t leave any space for countries not to adopt these 59 indicators. These are complex and incomplete, which means most countries aren’t happy with them.” Parties agreed on the need for a “two-tier” approach to resolving this, with a taskforce undertaking technical work on the indicators and then a policy alignment process for testing them. However, the composition of the taskforce quickly became a sticking point, just as it had in Bonn earlier in the year, according to ENB .  The 19 November draft GGA text still contained three options on the taskforce’s composition, including a mix of experts nominated either by regions, the chairs of the UNFCCC subsidiary bodies or by UN organisations and other non-party stakeholders.  Parties also disagreed on references in the GGA text to the Paris Agreement and “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities” ( CBDR-RC ), plus on recognition of the importance of the 1.5C goal in limiting the need for adaptation.  While the final decision agreed at COP31 does not mention overshoot or 1.5C, it does provide clarity on the taskforce. It “agrees” that six experts will be nominated per UN regional group, in addition to three experts nominated by the LDCs and three by small island developing states.  With so much time and focus given to the finance question, smaller technical aspects of the GGA negotiations struggled to find consensus across the two weeks of COP31.  Laughlin said:  “I think we are seeing these big-number finance issues as absolutely fundamental, but we’re also seeing the technical elements of the process, where the real work of implementation is done, be significantly challenged and, in my view, denigrated into obsolescence.” Observers told Carbon Brief that there had not been sufficient time given to the GGA, as well as items such as national adaptation plans (NAPs). One said that more than double the negotiating time had been devoted to the cover decision than to mandated items, such as the GGA, MWP and JTWP, over the first week.  Beauchamp told Carbon Brief she hoped that COP32 president Ethiopia would “break this pattern”.  Beyond the GGA, other adaptation items also proved challenging at COP31.  G77 and China huddle during informal consultations on national adaptation plans. Source: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis. The adaptation fund is the oldest dedicated UN climate fund and was set up as part of the 1992 UN climate convention. Now, it is in the process of transitioning to exclusively serve the 2015 Paris Agreement. This will allow it to access 5% of the revenues generated by the agreement’s Article 6.4 carbon market.  This process has previously been delayed by disagreements over the makeup of the fund’s board.  Under the Paris Agreement, the board would have set quotas for “developed” and “developing” nations – the terms used in the treaty – instead of  “Annex I” and “non-Annex I” nations, as it has done in the past.  Some parties see this distinction as important, because the UNFCCC annexes clearly separate a small group of predominantly European and industrialised states from other nations, whereas the “developed-developing” division is less clearly defined. Joe Thwaites , international climate finance director at Natural Resources Defense Council , told Carbon Brief that parties “can’t access” the Article 6.4 “share of proceeds” until this is resolved. A draft text released on 18 November continued to include references to both “developed countries” and parties “included in Annex I to the convention” within square brackets.  Ultimately, the final decision adopted “developed” and “developing country” language, but it also confirmed that developing countries will continue to have a majority of seats on the board.  Thwaites described the resolution of the adaptation fund negotiations as “one bright spot” from the climate summit, noting: “The decisions at COP31 enable the fund to receive a share of carbon-trading proceeds under the Paris Agreement crediting mechanism, which will not be subject to the politics of national budget processes.”  Negotiations on NAPs , adaptation communications and adaptation committee discussions all ended with procedural conclusions, meaning no substantive agreement was reached.  One adaptation area with more progress was “matters relating to the LDCs”, an agenda item where parties discuss support and adaptation planning for the 44 LDCs .   Despite “difficult negotiations”, on the second Wednesday of COP31, parties agreed to a decision that establishes a “LDCs national adaptation plan implementation platform” under the LDCs expert group.  ENB quoted a delegate saying: “This decision may not make the headlines, but it means a lot for the more than one billion most vulnerable people who benefit from the work under this agenda item.” Finance As COP31 ended in disputes and finger-pointing, a major complaint by many parties was the failure to agree progress on climate finance. In their closing speeches, several developing-country figures expressed “profound concern”, accusing developed countries of “refusing to engage” on this “essential” issue.  Finance talks ended with little – beyond decisions to hold more meetings. There was no progress on “tripling adaptation finance”, despite efforts to flesh out this goal. (See: Adaptation .)  Finance negotiations took place amid major aid cuts by developed countries and, as revealed by Carbon Brief, a corresponding 70% drop in the amount of public climate funding being pledged. COP31 co-president Australia drew heavy criticism from NGOs for failing to commit new funds, along with other major donors, such as Germany, France and Japan.  Meanwhile, pledges to UN climate funds fell to their lowest levels in years, with few new commitments in Antalya.  Protesters at COP31 calling for climate finance. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Two years ago, nations agreed on a “ new collective quantified goal ” (NCQG), which involves developed countries “taking the lead” in raising $300bn in climate finance a year by 2035. A variety of sources are expected to feed into this goal, including multilateral development banks , UN climate funds and private finance “mobilised” by public investments.  In recent years, roughly a third of total climate finance has been public finance from developed countries. The provision of funds by these nations now looks less certain , amid economic struggles and pressure to raise military spending. Developing countries, therefore, came to COP31 looking for assurances. Finance was discussed across most rooms in Antalya, but negotiations around a climate finance “ work programme ” – set up at COP30 last year – were the main venue for this push. Developing countries had wanted to create this space to discuss finance “provision” under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which says developed countries “shall provide” finance. This is taken to mean public funding – such as aid spending – from developed countries. (The NCQG, on the other hand, is a “mobilisation” goal, meaning it covers various funding sources, including private finance “mobilised” by public investments.) This came amid concerns that developed countries were trying to transfer responsibility onto others. They also argued for an extensive new set of talks and other activities. Extract from “work programme on climate finance” text from 15 November, showing an option for “burden-sharing arrangements”. Credit: UNFCCC . Such ideas were unacceptable for developed countries, who generally wanted a far more limited set of actions that were “non-prescriptive” and “non-punitive”.  They argued that the talks should be based on the existing $300bn mobilisation goal, stressing that they were already contributing tens of billions a year. Speaking at the climate summit, Hoekstra told Carbon Brief: “We made a deal with the whole world community on financing…We don’t think there is any merit in opening it.” (The work programme was established “without prejudging the process for the implementation of the NCQG”.) This would mean adaptation finance coming from both their public spending and other sources . In particular, the EU, the UK and others said they wanted to discuss “access” – helping small islands and other low-capacity nations to better get hold of the finance that already exists. Article 6 Negotiations at COP31 on carbon trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement reopened many familiar arguments over how tightly such activities should be regulated. Beatriz Granziera , senior policy adviser at The Nature Conservancy (TNC), told Carbon Brief: “Discussions repeatedly came back to familiar trade-offs: practicality versus conservativeness; flexibility versus oversight; and how to scale much-needed participation and investment while maintaining environmental integrity.” Agreement was, ultimately, reached on both bilateral trading under Article 6.2 and the international carbon market under Article 6.4. Carbon trading between countries under Article 6.2 is only subject to light-touch rules, such as reporting on the use of the process and a “technical expert review” of national reports. Across 16 national reports checked so far, these reviews found 543 “inconsistencies”, 115 of which were “significant”. None of the reports were found to be without issue. An initial draft text at Antalya “note[d these issues] with concern”, adding that “many…are significant” and relate to “environmental integrity” – in other words, whether or not emissions are actually being cut. It asked parties to address issues “at the earliest opportunity”. However, this entire paragraph disappeared in the final, agreed text . Instead, the decision “takes note” of the information in the technical reports, without asking for any response. Given its confidentiality provisions, campaign groups have long described Article 6.2 as a “ wild west ” for carbon trading and the COP31 outcome does nothing to tighten the rules. Separately, parties were unable to reach agreement at COP31 on how to fund the processes needed to run Article 6.2. Instead, they agreed to continue discussions next year, requesting a technical paper on how “fees or other funding arrangements” would work. Response measures Talks on “response measures” were some of the least contentious at COP31, however, the final plenary still rejected a draft decision on the topic.  At UN climate talks, “ response measures ” is a forum for discussing the effects of carbon-cutting policies on countries. They are particularly relevant for nations where controls on emissions or deforestation pose a risk to communities and the economy.  In recent years, the forum has been where trade and climate issues have been discussed.  In 2024, COP29 in Baku established a four-year work plan on response measures, including the “cross-border impacts” of climate-change measures. This created a formal space to discuss and assess trade-related climate measures in UN climate talks.  COP30 in Belém established a two-day “global dialogue” on response measures each year from 2026-29. The first was in Bangkok from 21-22 September 2026, focusing on economic diversification and on how to manage impacts on vulnerable populations. COP31 also conducted its first annual ministerial high-level round table on response measures on 17 November. Credit: Kubilay Ciftci / UNFCCC In Antalya, three key disputes emerged. The first was on what activities the forum would undertake in 2027 and, second, how it would consider recommendations from its Katowice Committee (KCI) of experts. The third was on whether – and how – response measures would inform the second “ global stocktake ”. At the start of negotiations, countries – including the African group, AOSIS, South Korea and China – called for a wide range of activities next year. One of these included a new “cross-border” impact assessment of response measures. On 16 November, the EU suggested removing an activity that refers to Article 3.5 of the 1992 UN climate convention, covering trade and an “open international economic system”.  Eventually, countries settled on four different activities. These include a workshop next June for the most affected countries to learn how to report these impacts, plus another workshop at COP32 on “technological solutions” to reduce climate impacts. As work on the second global stocktake (GST2) gets underway, countries disagreed on how response measures would feed into it. As of 19 November , the same four options remained on the table, including one with “no text”.  One option, supported by G77 and China, “decide[d]” that all of the outputs of the forum – dialogues, workshops, technical reports and case studies – would serve as substantive inputs to GST2.  This option “urged” that the cross-border impact assessment be conducted “before and during” GST2, including metrics such as inflation, trade flows, household income, employment and debt. Canada and the EU warned that this would change the global stocktake’s “well-established function”, reported Earth Negotiations Bulletin .  However, Switzerland, Norway, EU and the UK supported a compromise option – where countries could submit their views on the “social and economic impacts of response measures” as input to GST2.  Eventually, the option explicitly containing a cross-border impact assessment as an input to  GST2 was deleted from the final draft .   Instead, the text “recognises” that inputs to GST2 are “non-exhaustive” and “affirms” that all the forum’s outputs will feed into the stocktake’s technical assessment. This includes work on cross-border impacts – including trade measures – and how to report and analyse them. At the same time, it “invites” countries to submit their views on the “social and economic consequences” of response measures by 28 February 2027, which would also inform the stocktake. During the final plenary, the EU told delegates it objected to the adoption of the decision on response measures, on the grounds that it “contains provisions that are highly problematic”, as well as “the lack of recognition of the best available science”.  This was supported by Canada and the UK, with the latter adding: “We cannot accept any outcome that seeks to undermine and unduly influence the next global stocktake.” Brazil and Saudi Arabia both expressed their disappointment with the rejection of the text. Brazil said that the draft “excludes the voices of developing countries, the very countries that struggle to address the social and economic impacts of mitigation measures”. It asked for a formal note that the role and mandate of the forum were being “undermined”. Action for climate empowerment A draft decision on “ action for climate empowerment ” (ACE) had been set for adoption at COP31, but was unexpectedly torpedoed by Russia in the closing plenary. This area of the negotiations aims to encourage people to engage in climate action in different ways – through education, training, public awareness and access to information. COP27 had agreed to a four-year “action plan” on ACE that ends this year. COP31 was due to have agreed a new plan for 2027-2031, with some parties wanting it to address “misinformation and disinformation” related to climate change. During the Antalya talks, Russia, along with Saudi Arabia and Paraguay, objected to including a reference to countering climate-related “misinformation and disinformation”, reported ENB . It added that Russia described this as amounting to the censorship of other scientific views. Russia also made repeated efforts to replace previously agreed language on “gender-responsive” action with the phrase “gender-sensitive”. A draft decision , proposed by the presidency on 21 November, “note[d] the need to enhance efforts to promote and support the integrity of information on climate change”. The proposal also “recognise[d] the centrality of equity and the best available science for effective climate action and policymaking, as provided by the IPCC”. It then set out an action plan for continued work from 2027-2031. Notably, while references to “misinformation” had been removed, it still talked of “ensuring that the public has access to reliable, accurate climate information and is equipped with adequate climate literacy skills”. Draft text for the ACE “action plan”, published 21 November. Source: UNFCCC . During the closing plenary, however, Russia said it “reject[ed]” the “censorship of science” and that it “objected” to the draft text on action for climate empowerment. It said discussions had been “held hostage by considerations which are not part of the climate process”. The EU and the UK for the Umbrella group expressed their “surprise” at Russia’s objection. The UK said this topic was “very important for our group” and that “respect for gender equality and all identities is core to an effective, inclusive and meaningful process”. The COP president told the plenary that, “in light of the objection from the Russian Federation”, the issue of action for climate for empowerment would be deferred until the Bonn talks in June 2027. In a statement, campaign group Climate Action Against Disinformation said: “The ACE action plan should have been a milestone for truth at COP31. Instead, the Russian federation – the epicentre of climate disinformation – blocked its adoption, standing alone against 193 other[s].” Trade After the creation of three annual “dialogues” on trade within the COP30 Belém “global mutirão” decision, the topic was not expected to feature on the official agenda, even if it was likely to come up in other negotiating tracks. But, in the end, the rejection of not only the cover decision, but also agreements on “response measures” and agriculture, meant that trade was entirely missing from the COP31 outcome. (See: Response measures and Agriculture .) (A request from the African group to add trade to the COP31 agenda was also rejected .) Trade and climate featured strongly in the first “ reflections ” text on a cover decision, which was a compilation of suggestions from parties. Paragraph 119 of the first draft “call[ed] on” developed countries to “phase out unilateral…trade-restrictive measures” by the end of 2027. Commonly cited examples of what this might refer to include the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism and deforestation law. (See: Agriculture and food security .) First draft of the COP31 cover decision. Source: UNFCCC The phase-out call was, expectedly, cut from the second iteration of the cover text.    Speaking to Carbon Brief, global policy advisor at Greenpeace East Asia Yao Zhe said: “No one thought it would survive, probably even the ones [who] proposed it. But I see it as an indication that [countries] are persistent in pushing the trade angle.” Yao added that she expected China, with the African group, to “aim for higher” on trade at next year’s COP32 summit. In the end, with the “Antalya pact” failing, none of the references to trade survived the conference. In the closing plenary, Russia, Venezuela, Brazil, Iran, Kenya – with the Arab and African groups – lamented how the issue of trade was treated in the talks, with Saudi Arabia saying developing countries were told “this is a matter that is completely off the table”. Russia’s representative remarked that “climate policy should not turn into trade policy by other means”, calling customs tariffs on “green” supply chains “old colonial distribution of labour under a new green banner.” Ghana, for the African group, pointed out “no firm treatment” of trade measures at COP31. Credit: Mike Muzurakis / Earth Negotiations Bulletin Ghana and Kenya both flagged the lack of “firm treatment” of trade measures and hinted that it would be a priority for them at COP32. Kenya’s delegate said: “Unilateral trade measures are only noted. African economies bear their costs, while the decision merely notes their views.”  Second global stocktake Against a backdrop of fraught negotiations, the second “ global stocktake ” (GST) was launched at a high-level event in the middle of the second week of COP31. The GST is the Paris Agreement’s five-yearly “ reality check ”, measuring whether the world’s collective efforts are enough to sufficiently cut emissions and prepare for climate impacts. The first stocktake culminated in Dubai at COP28 in 2023, resulting in the first-ever global commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels ”, among various other pledges. GST2 will run until 2028, meaning COP33 will have to address the likely shortfall between the Paris Agreement’s goals and reality. An important question hanging over this process is whether parties will have access to the latest IPCC science in time for the second GST, as a small group of countries push for the next IPCC report to be published after the stocktake. (See: Cover text. ) COP31 also featured a “dialogue” on how the lessons of the first GST could inform countries’ future NDCs.  Parties such as the EU and climate-vulnerable nations argued for a more substantial outcome that included guidance for the second GST and references to the 1.5C target. This was opposed by many developing countries. In the end, parties decided on a procedural outcome without any of the more ambitious language that had appeared in previous drafts . Long-term goal review COP31 was unable to agree on whether to start a third “periodic review” of the UN climate convention ’s long-term goal and progress towards meeting it. The goal of the 1992 convention is to avoid “dangerous” climate change, a target that was defined at COP16 in 2010 as a warming limit of 2C. COP16 also said that this goal – and progress towards meeting it – should be subject to “periodic review”. The first review , in 2013-2015, helped secure the Paris 1.5C limit. At the start of the second review at COP25 , some parties disputed the need for the process, given the existence of five-yearly “ global stocktakes ” of progress under the Paris Agreement. Underlying this disagreement is the fact that the convention has distinct country requirements for developed and developing parties, whereas the Paris regime does not. Discussions on a third review stalled at COP29 and continued at COP30. Some developed countries said it was “ redundant ”, while developing countries wanted it to continue. In Antalya, countries were split over whether to begin a third periodic review, whether to delay it until publication of the next IPCC report, or whether to discontinue the process. The final COP31 text “notes the consideration” of the matter and decides to continue talking at COP32 next year. At the first closing plenary , China, along with India for the LMDCs and Saudi Arabia for the Arab group, expressed their “concern” over the lack of agreement. China said: “We are seriously concerned that some developed country parties…in the name of streamlined process…substantively tried to terminate this mechanism.” For AOSIS, Palau “regret[ted]” the lack of progress on what it said was the “only dedicated space to reflect on the 1.5C limit on the basis of substantive scientific input”. Guidance on NDCs COP31 was unable to agree on further guidance for countries when preparing their climate pledges under the Paris Agreement, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). This issue has been disputed in the past, with talks also failing at COP29 in Baku two years ago. In Antalya, parties were once again split over whether to issue further guidance Developed and vulnerable countries – including the EU and small island states – want more guidance, to prompt stronger implementation and more transparent pledges. The LMDCs, the Arab group and African group, prefer to avoid what they see as prescriptive further guidance that could impinge on the “nationally determined” nature of the documents. The negotiations were subject to “ rule 16 ”, meaning they ended without agreement and will resume at the next session of the talks in Bonn next June. Rio synergies To the dismay of many countries, negotiations on the need for “synergies” between the three Rio conventions of climate change, biodiversity loss and land desertification ended with the adoption of just a one-line text .  The text simply states that, during negotiations under this item – known as “cooperation with other international organisations” – there was an “exchanges of views” and an agreement to “continue consideration at the next session”. The agreed text for the “cooperation with other international organisations” agenda item. Source: UNFCCC . On 10 November – the second day of COP – ENB reported that Russia, supported by the Arab group, “opposed continuing the discussion” on Rio synergies. Speaking on the behalf of 14 small island developing states in plenary on 14 November, Fiji said it was “deeply disappointed” by the outcome. It told delegates: “We came to Antalya ready to advance cooperation across Rio conventions and to foster synergies in national implementation. That is what all parties agreed to do when we left Bonn . We did not do that. Not because the issues were too difficult, but because we were never permitted to discuss them in the way we intended to do so. “At the very first informal consultation, before a single substantive proposal had been heard, the intention to invoke ‘ rule 16 ’ was announced by one group of party. We offered repeatedly to address any and all concerns. That offer was not taken up. Substantive discussion was blocked from the very first hour to the last.” The EIG, Panama for AILAC, the UK for the Umbrella group and the EU all expressed similar disappointment. Around the COP Fossil fuels The issue of “transitioning away from fossil fuels” dominated again at COP31, with countries leaving the talks still deeply divided on how it should be taken forward. Including “transitioning away from fossil fuels” in the cover decision was one of the key asks of a group of 126 countries spanning Europe, the small island states, parts of Latin America and the Caribbean and other major developed countries. In the end, several countries rejected the proposed cover decision over its lack of a clear reference to fossil fuels, with the EU saying: “We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” Fossil fuels also featured prominently on the sidelines at COP, with more than 80 side events and talks dedicated to the topic, Carbon Brief understands. In addition, eight European and small island nations announced intentions to release national roadmaps away from fossil fuels – bringing the total number with such plans up to 27. The first major event on fossil fuels took place on the summit’s second day, when the Brazilian COP30 presidency formally presented its global fossil-fuel roadmap to a packed-out plenary room.
