In Antalya, COP30 president André Corrêa do Lago told delegates that the roadmap is “not a mandate” and “not related to the negotiations”. Instead, he said, “it’s contribution and input for the implementation that we need to do”. The session featured key figures, including UN secretary general António Guterres, UN climate chief Simon Stiell, COP26 president Alok Sharma and former US climate envoy John Kerry. However, COP31 presidents Kurum and Bowen were conspicuously absent. The next day, during his speech at the world leaders’ summit, Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva called on Turkey and Australia to “ensure that the recommendations contained in [the roadmaps] are disseminated and incorporated into the next global stocktake ”. On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This included a bullet point saying some parties would like to see “transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems” included in the text. (This language was first agreed by countries as part of the first global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai in 2023.) On the same day, Irene Vélez Torres, Colombia’s former environment minister, told journalists that a mere repetition of language agreed in Dubai would not represent progress for many parties. Vélez Torres co-led a first-of-its-kind conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta in April this year, which was attended by 57 countries. She told the huddle that, regardless of what is agreed by consensus on fossil fuels at COP31, countries committed to transitioning away would continue to take action, saying: “Consensus as a method is not going to stop us anymore…we know it has limited ambition. It is limiting implementation, but this is not going to stop us.” On Monday 16 November, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “ presidency note ” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text.  One part of this draft “call[ed] for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”. Another part of the text also “welcome[d]” the Brazil-led global roadmaps on the transition away from fossil fuels and on ending deforestation. The next day, a group of European and small island state ministers held a press conference on the need to transition away from fossil fuels. Denmark, Spain, Portugal and Luxembourg announced that they intend to release new national roadmaps away from fossil fuels.  (Earlier that day, Vanuatu had announced its own national roadmap and the development of a Pacific regional roadmap away from fossil fuels.)  Speaking as a united front, the group of ministers called for the language on fossil fuels contained within the first draft to be strengthened and given more prominence. However, Carbon Brief understands that, behind-the-scenes, hopes that any kind of fossil-fuel language would survive into the second draft cover decision were fast evaporating. On 18 November, a group of global-south ministers held a press conference, attended by Carbon Brief, to show their support for transitioning away from fossil fuels. At the event, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and Guatemala announced that they were joining the fossil fuel treaty , an initiative to develop a legal instrument to control fossil fuels. This brought the total number of countries supporting the treaty up to 30. During the press conference, Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro made headlines with an explosive speech, telling journalists that the world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia”. The next day, the co-hosts of the second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference – Tuvalu and Ireland – held a press conference. They confirmed that a pre-conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels would be held in Dublin in May, with the actual conference taking place in Tuvalu in July. Speaking at the press conference, Tuvalu climate minister Maina Talia publicly acknowledged he was not expecting to see transitioning away from fossil fuels in the second draft of the cover decision. The co-hosts also confirmed that a third transitioning away from fossil fuels conference will be held in 2028. (Lula told civil society at COP that Brazil was keen to host it. Carbon Brief understands Cambodia and Ghana are also interested.) Later that day, a second draft cover decision was published. It did not mention “fossil fuels” at all, nor “paragraph 28 of decision 1/CMA.5”, the passage of text from the first global stocktake that calls for countries to contribute to “transitioning away from fossil fuels”. In the evening, Kurum and Bowen held a press conference to defend their second draft and tried to bat away questions from journalists about whether the removal of fossil-fuel language represented “backsliding”. Both presidents cited their push to get countries to sign up to electrification as complementary to transitioning away from fossil fuels, with Bowen telling journalists: “The world agreed at COP28 to transition away from fossil fuels. What we’re about is practical ways to do that. There’s no better way than electrification.”  However, it was widely understood that many countries were not happy with the omission of fossil fuels. Guatemala, Belgium and Switzerland were also on the stage. As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update on the state of the text failed to materialise.  Tuvalu’s Talia told a cramped press huddle that Pacific island nations had been waiting for the text since last night and were still willing to fight to get transitioning away from fossil fuels back in. Maina Vakafua Talia, Tuvalu’s climate minister, speaks to journalists. Credit: Sandro Basili / Alamy Stock Photo On Saturday evening, the fallout over fossil fuels intensified.  Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UG, AOSIS, AILAC and LDCs – approached the presidency as a united front to demand that transitioning away from fossil fuels featured in the final cover decision. One observer told Carbon Brief that such close cooperation between the EU and AOSIS is “unprecedented” at COP. They added that it might reflect the fact that Ireland, which currently holds the EU presidency, is working closely with Tuvalu on holding the second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference next year. A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.  This one also did not directly mention fossil fuels. However, it did “recall” the COP28 UAE consensus “in its entirety”, which itself includes a reference to a “just, orderly and equitable” transition away from fossil fuels. Carbon Brief contributing editor Dr Joanna Depledge wrote on LinkedIn that this oblique reference was “near meaningless”. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, many countries rejected the text – citing its failure to clearly reference transitioning away from fossil fuels as one of the key reasons. (See: Cover decision .) Action agenda Many issues that were intensely negotiated at COP31 – including the electrification goal and fossil-fuel phaseout – also featured in the “ action agenda ”. This is the part of the UN climate process that involves mobilising real-world climate action from non-state actors, including businesses, investors and civil-society groups.  It also covers voluntary actions taken by groups of countries beyond the COP negotiations. When the “Antalya pact” failed to materialise, the presidency’s action agenda package was one of its more substantial outputs.  In this closing remarks at COP31, after the headline negotiated outcome had collapsed, UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell reminded delegates: “This COP process has two tracks. And across the action agenda, COP31 has delivered real progress and concrete results.” With Australia overseeing negotiations, the action agenda was instead a priority for the Turkish presidency, which used COP31 to launch a variety of new projects and “ compacts ”. In a phrase familiar to attendees of previous COPs , Turkish COP31 president Murat Kurum said he wanted an “implementation COP” that would leave people saying: “Something changed in Antalya.” Delegates resting by a wall with the COP31 slogan “dialogue, consensus, action”. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Amid global conflict, struggling multilateralism and the imminent breaching of the 1.5C Paris Agreement goal, UN climate talks have repeatedly failed to reach consensus on vital issues. Some have, therefore , welcomed what the Brazilian COP30 presidency called “two-tier multilateralism”, in which parties try to find consensus where they can and, where they cannot, coalitions of willing nations and groups push more ambitious action forward. Kaveh Guilanpour , vice president for international strategies at the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES), told Carbon Brief: “There’s a lot of inertia in the formal way of negotiating and we’re trying to find our way to whatever that new thing is, given the foundational era of negotiations is over.” Last year, the Brazilian presidency consolidated hundreds of existing climate initiatives – including many launched at previous COPs – into a streamlined set that could be supported and tracked under the action agenda. This included setting out more than 120 “ plans to accelerate solutions ”, to advance everything from phasing out coal to ending food waste. Tracking by UN Climate Change found that 104 of these plans had seen progress over the past year. By the end of COP31, the total number of plans had increased to 136, with new ones filling “ important gaps ”, such as early warning systems . Crucially, the plans were structured to align with the global stocktake outcomes from COP28 – such as curbing fossil fuels and tripling renewables – which all nations agreed on.  In this way, the revised action agenda is intended to explicitly support negotiated outcomes. Turkey announced 10 “ priority themes ” for the COP31 action agenda, fitting them into the existing framework. By far the most high profile was the “electrification” focus. (See: Electrification .) A book distributed at the summit by the Turkish presidency stated that a “large number of events, declarations and partnerships does not by itself constitute implementation success”. Nevertheless, the presidency did launch many new initiatives, including six voluntary 2035 targets that countries and non-state actors could sign up for.  These included “compacts” to curb the “ energy intensity ” of buildings by 25% and increase the use of “circular materials” in manufacturing to at least 15% by 2035. These initiatives attracted dozens of backers, but gained far less support than the electrification goal. Other notable initiatives pushed by the Turkish presidency include a domestic pledge for “ zero waste districts ” and an “ Antalya artificial intelligence (AI) pledge ”, which focused on curbing data-centre emissions while advancing “AI solutions for climate action”. COP31 also saw progress on two initiatives launched by COP30’s “ global mutirão ” decision that are relevant for the growth of the action agenda. The first was the “ Belém mission to 1.5 ”, which identified key priority areas for countries to meet their climate goals.  The second was the “ global implementation accelerator ”, which was formally established at COP31. This involves presidencies and experts choosing two action-agenda plans each year that are best placed to drive “ positive tipping points ” for climate action.  Cosima Cassel , E3G climate diplomacy lead, told Carbon Brief that this focus, “based on science, not just on the presidency’s priorities…is an extra step in the evolution of the action agenda”. Global climate action high-level event. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . During a COP31 session on the “accelerator”, COP30 strategy director Túlio Andrade said the Brazilian team wanted it to advance the transition “from a negotiation-focused regime to one very much focused on implementation”. The Turkish presidency also announced a new project called the “ climate implementation bridge ”, while pledging an initial $3m to support its operations. In partnership with the UN Development Programme, the bridge’s goal is to turn nations’ climate plans into “ bankable projects ” and connect them with finance.  Together, the “mission”, “accelerator” and “bridge” form part of a wider “ ecosystem ” that supporters hope will identify and support priority areas of climate action. However, the growing profile of the action agenda has resulted in pushback, with India and the Arab group arguing against any mention of it in formal negotiations. In contrast, Brazil accused the presidency of failing to significantly acknowledge these “concrete instruments and initiatives” in the proposed “Antalya pact”.  Some parties and observers are concerned that the action agenda is a diversion from parties’ obligations under UN climate treaties, such as providing climate finance. Arguing that the focus should instead be on reforming the COP process, Vanuatu climate minister Ralph Regenvanu told Carbon Brief: “Unfortunately, the action agenda has not necessarily led to action. It is indicative, again, that the COP process is broken. While people innovating and coming together to take action is good, it cannot take the place of negotiations.” Developing countries, which often have far fewer delegates , also struggle to follow all the additional activities. In a closing session , Stiell invited parties to nominate focal points so that the UN could help to “connect them with action agenda opportunities all year round”. Guilanpour noted that while “everybody says they want to focus on implementation”, within the traditional COP process this can only apply to “a very rarefied subset of obligations”, such as submitting revised NDCs. He added: “When the rest of the world hears implementation, they want to see pollution in their city going down, their energy bills going down…and that sort of implementation is in the action agenda.” Global leaders COP31’s world leaders’ summit took place during the conference’s first week from 11-12 November. Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – whose recent re-election was widely interpreted as a timely boost for climate action and multilateralism by delegates – gave a blistering speech in the summit’s opening ceremony. He told other world leaders: “We have started talking more about weapons and tariffs than about the survival of future generations…But the planet cannot be left at the mercy of hegemonic disputes.” He told leaders that he wanted COP30 , which took place last year in the Brazilian city of Belém, to be remembered as the “COP of truth” – but that “science and multilateralism remain under attack”, adding: “It is not by chance that the incorporation of IPCC contributions into the COP negotiation process is in question. Nor is it a coincidence that climate agreements are the favourite targets of reactionary forces at COPs.” He also touted Brazil’s newly released global roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation , urging COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia to “ensure that the recommendations contained in these documents are disseminated and incorporated into the next global stocktake ”. In one of his final addresses in the role, UN secretary general António Guterres said that the “brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us”, adding: “Leaders – and, in particular, those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil-fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C.” Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdoğan used his address to call on developed countries to “take greater responsibility for emission reductions and financing” and to call out “ecocide” in Gaza. (Erdoğan faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields in Turkey on the eve of the summit.) Barbados prime minister Mia Mottley cited Carbon Brief analysis to reprimand developed countries in her address to the world leaders’ summit, telling the room: ”My friends, let us be clear: pledges are not payments. But even the promised pledges are now 70% below previous levels.” UK prime minister Andy Burnham, the only G7 leader to attend the summit, said that electrification is “how we make clean power cheap power”. He also announced the appointment of the country’s first special representative on climate security.  In total, around 70 world leaders spoke at the summit – with many major polluters missing. For the second year, the US did not send any delegates to COP. (Donald Trump took the US out of the Paris Agreement and the UN climate treaty after returning to office.) However, success for Democrats in the US midterm elections, shortly before COP31, lifted hopes that the world’s second-largest emitter could one day return to the talks. “America is all in” – a coalition of mostly Democratic governors, Congress members and local mayors – had a pavilion at COP31 and brought around 120 delegates (a figure larger than many official country delegations ). Speaking on 16 November at a pavilion event attended by Carbon Brief, Jared Huffman , a Democratic Congressional representative from California, said that the midterm results were a “clear rejection” of Trump’s “climate denial” and “wrecking ball to climate and energy policy”. He added: “The next time that we are here at a COP, it will be different…We will be an official Congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives. And soon after that, this yellow part of our lanyard that says ‘observer’ will change and the US will truly be officially back in as part of the negotiati[ons].” Other countries without delegations at the talks included Myanmar and Israel, according to Carbon Brief analysis. Electrification Amid a global energy crisis driven by disruption in the trade of fossil fuels, one of the biggest themes of COP31 was electrification.  Much attention was focused on which nations had signed up to a voluntary pledge to “increase the share of electricity in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035”.  For much of COP31, this was expected to be one of the main outcomes in the “Antalya pact” cover text, which ultimately failed to find agreement among parties. (See: Cover decision .) Nevertheless, some countries made public pledges of support for the target during the COP, including in a joint China-Australia statement .  COP31 president Murat Kurum told the closing plenary that “around 80” countries were behind the goal, but a full list was never published. The pledge was launched earlier in the year as a “flagship initiative of the COP31 presidency’s action agenda” – part of its wider goal to “ electrify the world ”. (See: Action agenda .) As explained on CB Connect , it drew from analysis by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), which was explicitly designed to align with the 1.5C target and support the Brazilian COP30 presidency’s “roadmap” for transitioning away from fossil fuels.  Ministers and representatives from Papua New Guinea, Antigua and Barbuda, Zambia, Germany, the Philippines and Colombia hold connected extension cables in a demonstration of their support for electrification. Credit: Carbon Brief. Towards the end of COP31, the presidency launched its “ electrification delivery package ”, capturing 14 newly announced international initiatives and other relevant projects. Among them were an industry-backed “maritime electrification goal” to increase electricity’s share of shipping’s final energy demand to 20% by 2035, as well as projects to boost grid investment, renewables in small-island states and transitions away from coal. One notable initiative was the Electrify Now Finance Coalition – launched with the backing of the COP31 and COP32 presidencies – to “mobilise over $1.2bn for clean electrification projects” in developing countries. At a coalition launch event, featuring ministers from Ethiopia, Germany, Pakistan and several other nations, Bruce Douglas , chief executive of the Global Renewables Alliance , told attendees that at least 25 nations had already put in place policies to drive electrification since the start of the “ Hormuz crisis ”. He said: “We now have the formula for success: renewable energy plus electrification equals secure, affordable and clean energy for all consumers.” China at COP31 Closing COP31 with a signal of “solidarity and multilateralism” was “more important than specific problems”, said China at the opening plenary of the summit. Its climate officials said repeatedly that not every COP required a “ new outcome ” and noted the need to “ manage expectations ”.  These comments seemed prescient when negotiations broke down at the end of COP31 over the cover decision . China had outlined its key aims for COP31 in a press conference held by Li Gao, vice-minister of ecology and environment and delegation head, in late October. These were primarily to commit developed countries to do more on mitigation and finance, as well as to address “unilateralism and protectionism” in the trade of clean-energy technologies. But Li also “commend[ed]” the presidency’s call for countries to pledge to achieve a 35% share of electricity in global final energy consumption by 2035. One of the biggest questions hovering over the COP was whether China would officially support the pledge, which was incorporated into the failed cover text .  While observers had told Carbon Brief from early in the negotiations that it would be very likely that China would support the pledge in some form, the strongest signal came from a joint statement published with Australia in the second week. In it, the two countries “welcome[d] growing international ambition and cooperation on electrification…on a voluntary basis”, mentioning the 35 by 35 goal, as well as recognising various climate, social and economic benefits from the transition. (See: Electrification .)  China-Australia joint statement on climate change and the clean energy transition, published 20 November. Source: State Council of the People’s Republic of China . The cover text had similarly sought to “recognise that electrification has significant benefits in terms of emission reductions, energy security, energy efficiency, economic development and energy access”. The joint statement, however, did not explicitly mention fossil fuels, rather it noted “countries have different transition pathways” and the “importance of secure, affordable, reliable and resilient energy systems during the transition”. Li Shuo , director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), told Carbon Brief that the “carefully curated” language helped “firm up” support for the electrification pledge – and broader language around energy – in the final draft.  China had published a joint climate statement with the EU ahead of COP30 , as well as ones with the US ahead of COPs including COP21 , COP26 and COP28 . But, unlike these agreements, the Australia-China joint statement “mostly confirms existing relatively unambitious negotiation points and does not advance ambitions” on issues including fossil fuels and decarbonising trade, argued Prof Christoph Nedopil Wang at the University of Queensland . He told Carbon Brief: “Symbolically, it would have been more meaningful to sign a more ambitious statement before COP negotiations began.” As talks broke down at the closing plenary, China endorsed the cover text’s final draft, noting that, although it has “some concerns about the content”, it chose to accept the decision to “push forward our process and show a message of unity and collective efforts”. On 23 November, China’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying:  “We express our disappointment regarding this outcome, but believe that confidence in the multilateral process should not be lost as a result.” “China was not the main blocker for the text”, said ASPI’s Li.  He added that, in his view, even if language around transitioning away from fossil fuels had been made stronger, China would have found it acceptable. China also tried to preserve the mitigation work programme (MWP) at the closing plenary. (See: Mitigation work programme .)  In negotiations, China joined other developing countries in supporting the work programme’s extension through to 2030.  Speaking on behalf of the LMDCs, China emphasised the value of the MWP, but said it needed to “focus on how to eliminate barriers of implementation”, according to Third World Network .  These included developed countries’ lack of mitigation action and financial support, as well as unilateral trade measures, it added.  China, on behalf of the LMDCs, tried to build consensus around the MWP at the closing plenary by suggesting deleting references to the first global stocktake. However, the suggestion was rejected by Russia. Meanwhile, China continued to emphasise the need for a gradual transition away from fossil fuels throughout the COP. “‘Phasing out fossil fuels’ [淘汰化石燃料] is merely a proposition of a small number of countries and has never constituted a consensus”, climate envoy Liu Zhenmin told the Paper .  He added that the energy transition required “gradually replacing fossil fuels” with clean energy over the course of “decades” and that phasing out fossil fuels should not “become a focal point of COP31 negotiations”. A few days later and thousands of miles away, the presidents of China, the US and Russia declared at the APEC Summit that the three countries “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products” in response to global energy shocks . The China delegation office at COP31 did not respond to Carbon Brief’s request for comment on this matter.  An early push to get trade on the agenda came not from China, but from the African group . In the end, the item was not included on the agenda, though it was raised by China in negotiations on the just transition work programme , adaptation fund and standing committee on finance . The China-Australia joint statement notes “measures taken to combat climate change should not constitute a means of arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination or a disguised restriction on international trade”. Prof Nedopil Wang told Carbon Brief that Australia would be more open to compromise on language with China around cleantech trade than the EU or US, as its economy has few “domestic substitutes for China’s manufactured products”. Text on trade measures were included in the cover decision drafts, though not adopted by parties. China did also focus significant attention on the just transition work programme, which was successfully passed. (See: Just transition work programme .) Speaking at a ministerial roundtable, environment vice-minister Li said that the “just transition is one of the most important agenda items of COP31” and must be operationalised.  In negotiations, China called for the mechanism to recognise the “north-south development gap” and a dedicated body to manage the programme – opposed by the EU. More broadly, the LMDCs urged that the work programme “avoid policy prescriptions” and not be linked to the global stocktake , which they argued would risk creating new obligations. Huang Runqiu, China’s minister for ecology and environment, speaking at a high-level event on the global implementation accelerator. Source: UNFCCC . Meanwhile, at a high-level dialogue on climate finance, watched by Carbon Brief, environment minister Huang Runqiu said that developed countries’ “climate finance commitments must be honoured and the financing gap narrowed”. Huang called for the new collective quantified goal (NCQG) to be “effectively implemented”, as well as for “establishing a common definition” for climate finance and improving accounting methodologies.  He additionally highlighted the need to improve the “quality of finance”, such as providing more grants and highly concessional loans, support for adaptation and easier access to climate finance. This was echoed by BASIC , who said that “developed countries must set a pathway towards the NCQG goal of $300bn annually” and triple adaptation finance. BASIC also said the climate finance work programme (CFWP) must “operationalise Article 9.1”. The final CFWP text was passed, but only focused on procedural matters, with mentions of tripling adaptation finance and “burden-sharing” in earlier drafts removed . Requests to expand the donor base were also deleted. China maintained its emphasis on Article 9.1 in a number of workstreams, notably through the CFWP and standing committee on finance. Carbon Brief understands that China was also one of two nations driving efforts to ensure that a dialogue on Article 2.1(c) , which ensures finance flows are “consistent” with climate action, remains open and non-binding. On adaptation finance, China underscored on behalf of the LMDCs the need to triple funds, calling for a “clear roadmap and timeline to increase the share of grants, as well as a progress-review mechanism”, said Third World Network . But, in general, ASPI’s Li says, “China’s position was right in the middle of the political spectrum” on most of the issues being negotiated, maintaining a “quiet, but self-assured posture”. An early point of discussion among delegates had been whether China could have signalled greater leadership at COP, such as by announcing a bid to host COP33. News emerged at COP31 that China had, after “ months ” of consideration, decided not to do so.  Prof Hu Bin , associate professor and director of global climate governance research at Tsinghua University ’s Institute of Climate Change and Sustainable Development, told Carbon Brief that “China, politically, is still very hesitant” to claim the role of the leading country on climate. Instead it is focusing on leading in terms of the transition on-the-ground he said, adding: “I still think the reason China doesn’t want to bid for COP33 is internal pressure – the economy is slowing down, local governments are facing lots of pressure for employment and for economic growth.”  Another way in which it was suggested China could display leadership was by helping create consensus around the IPCC’s AR7 report being published in time for the second global stocktake.  At an event at the China pavilion attended by Carbon Brief, Laurence Tubiana, key architect of the Paris Agreement, said she will “count on China to be the torchbearer for the world’s science at the second global stocktake”. But, at the same event, Prof Wang Yi argued that IPCC reports from AR1 to AR6 were “unequivocal that global warming is caused by human activity”. Wang is a professor at the Chinese Academy of Science and a lead advisor to the China delegation. This means the science is clear, “no matter” when AR7 is published, he added. China instead continued to position itself as a champion of the global south, both in negotiations and around the COP. In negotiations, it consistently aligned itself with developing country parties and groups, calling for solutions that would not “widen” the north-south gap. South-south cooperation was the subject of a high-level forum at which China’s vice-president Han Zheng spoke.  Han emphasised that “China will vigorously deepen south-south cooperation” and formally announced a new global south climate leadership training programme, according to a recording of the speech obtained by Carbon Brief. China also signed an agreement with Turkey to invest $15bn in developing 7GW of solar and wind power and 4GW of transmission capacity. This deal “could be seen as part of China’s own contribution to climate finance and accelerating the global energy transition”, even if it’s not “formally accounted”, said Kate Logan , director of the China Climate Hub and climate diplomacy at ASPI .  She added that, at a broader level, it shows that “China will continue exercising its influence through real-economy actions, even while its negotiators press for developed country accountability on finance”. Ocean Ocean advocates had several outcomes to celebrate at COP31 – and also some disappointment. Before the summit started, observers – and many parties – were hopeful of securing a strong outcome for the ocean, especially in light of the pre-COP meeting held in Pacific island states. A letter sent to the COP31 presidencies on 8 October – signed by the African group, the EU (along with its member states) and 24 other countries – called for the COP to “move sustainable ocean-based climate action from recognition to implementation”.  It said that such a move should be “backed by a clear political signal, a coherent plan for integration into the Paris Agreement ambition cycle and its existing means of implementation”. Analysis published by the World Resources Institute (WRI) on 15 November found that 95% of coastal and island countries included “at least one ocean-based action” in their national climate plans. However, it added that “more than 60% of ocean-commitment implementation depends on receiving some form of external support.” Two days later, on the “ocean, seas, nature and land use” thematic day, ministers from France and Brazil announced the launch of the “Blue NDC Challenge implementation task force” at a side event. They also welcomed 10 new countries as members of the Blue NDC Challenge – a group launched at the UN Ocean Conference in Nice, France, in June 2025 to “advance ocean-based climate action”. The same day, the COP31 presidency published the “Antalya Ocean and Seas Compact”, a high-level declaration that it said drew on feedback from parties and discussions at several events, including the UN General Assembly and the Pacific pre-COP.  The document highlights the impacts of climate change on the ocean, recognises the ocean’s importance in climate action and invites parties to strengthen their ocean work. The Antalya Ocean and Seas Compact. Source: COP31 presidency . Dr Tom Pickerell , global ocean programme director at WRI, told Carbon Brief: “It was more of a platform for collective ambition and political alignment, rather than any targets or finance coming through. We wouldn’t say no to it, but if we’d left just with that, it would have been a little bit sad.” Also on the ocean thematic day, the UK government announced a new £20m ($26.2m) funding commitment to marine protection. This comprised £11.8m ($15.5m) to the Global Fund for Coral Reefs and £9m ($11.8m) to the Global Ocean Accounts Partnership , which helps countries measure their progress towards sustainable ocean development. Towards the end of the summit, the “high-level climate-resilient coral reef commitment ” gained six new signatories: Colombia, Haiti, Jamaica, Niue, Samoa and Tuvalu. These governments “commit to protect[ing] reefs identified as having greater potential to persist through climate change”, according to a press release announcing the new countries. In the formal negotiation rooms, ocean groups were closely following discussions around the cover decision, hoping to see the ocean featured prominently there. (See: Cover decision .) Draft versions of the cover text “invite[d]” the development of a multi-year plan for future ocean and climate change dialogues, to be called the “Antalya ocean current”. It also asked for the results of these dialogues to be summarised, along with the “best available science” on the ocean, in a synthesis report that would act as an input to the second global stocktake. However, the cover decision was rejected during the closing plenary. Multiple parties used their interventions during the plenary to express their regret that the work that had been done on the ocean and climate change in the cover text would not move forward. Pickerell told Carbon Brief that while “it wasn’t a ‘blue COP’ after all”, there were still positive takeaways for the ocean. He said: “We’ve left with maybe nothing in writing, but I think we have left with genuine momentum. There does seem to be this shared ambition, to move beyond just the recognition of the ocean…There’s lots of opportunities to take this forward.” Deforestation COP31 was relatively quiet on forests, compared to last year’s summit in Belém.  The presidency held a forest leaders’ summit on 11 November, which was attended by the presidents of Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo, along with the prime ministers of the Netherlands and Norway. Much of the summit dwelled on the Brazil-led Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). Delegates speculated that the summit would yield major new pledges for the fund.  However, only $88m from philanthropies emerged as new contributions at the event. Several countries reiterated past and recent pledges.  Aruna Chandrasekhar 12 November 2026, 14:19 GMT Forest funding pledges fall short Plenary Akdeniz was ringing with applause and chants of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, Lula, Lula!” as Brazil’s president approached the stage for the forest leaders’ summit yesterday evening. Lula – who told the crowd he had lost his voice –… Read more on CB Connect → At the summit, Jonas Gahr Støre, Norway’s prime minister, said:  “I am hopeful we can reach our collective goal of mobilising the initial $10bn dollars and to increase from there through next year and, with this, Norway is ready to contribute up to 20% of that total.” Norway’s “up to $3bn” loan to the fund is conditional upon it hitting the $10bn mark by the end of 2026. At the same time, Støre acknowledged that “it will take some time before payments reach the tropical forest countries and the key people who we want to support”. Speaking at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila on 15 November, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney pledged “an initial contribution of up to” $393m over four years to the TFFF. This means the fund has – so far – mobilised $8.2bn from different international partners, mostly as conditional loans. This leaves it $1.8bn short of a $10bn target for public and philanthropic capital for this year.  Political economist Max Alexander Matthey told Carbon Brief that less capital to invest and fewer risks taken will “lead to a fund that will not be able to deliver on the initially promised $4 per hectare” of protected forest in participating countries, even in a best-case scenario.  Although significant attention was paid to the fossil-fuel roadmap at COP31, far less focus was given to the deforestation one. Chris Dragisic , managing director for global policy at the National Audubon Society , told Carbon Brief that, nonetheless, there were “a couple of countries” that committed to producing national forest roadmaps. She added: “Many others have said, ‘we have a national strategy already’, and they’re looking at this really as an option to accelerate progress…What, for me, is the more interesting thing is that the roadmap recatalysed political will across the board for forests, where these had fallen a little bit off the political radar.” Other forest-related commitments made at COP31 included Bolivia and Indonesia joining the Forest & Climate Leaders’ Partnership and Brazil’s announcement that it is working on an Indigenous peoples’ roadmap. The COP31 presidency also launched the voluntary “Antalya action plan” on global wildfires, which it said would help a “community of countries” to “cooperate on prevention, early warning, landscape resilience and access to resources”. On the penultimate scheduled day of the summit, more than 100 organisations – including Indigenous groups, civil society and research institutions – signed an open letter calling on countries to take the work of the deforestation roadmap forward. It also called for an “international convening” on deforestation to occur in 2027. While an initial draft of the cover text “welcome[d]” the Brazil-led roadmap on deforestation , this was subsequently cut.   The final cover text – which was rejected during the closing plenary – did retain wording on deforestation agreed by countries in the global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai. The text had also included a recognition of nature-based solutions as “essential climate solutions”, although there is significant controversy over their use. Language on deforestation included in the final, rejected draft of the COP31 cover decision. Source: UNFCCC . Methane Cutting emissions of methane , the potent but short-lived greenhouse gas, appeared to have a renewed push at COP31.  This is partly due to the recent confirmation of an “ inevitable ” overshoot of the 1.5C global temperature target . (See: Cover text .)    Inger Andersen , chief of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), referred to this at a COP31 methane event :  “[Methane] leaves the atmosphere quickly, so cutting its emissions is our emergency brake to slow warming.” It is “one of the fastest, cheapest and most effective ways to check global heating in the near-term ”, said UN climate chief Simon Stiell at a 12 November event on non-CO2 greenhouse gases.  At this event, UNEP announced that its methane alert system has flagged five methane leaks across Canada, Iraq, Kazakhstan and Mexico since June 2026, allowing those countries to mitigate 125,000 tonnes of methane.  New private funding of $480m (£366m) was also pledged for action on methane and other “ super pollutants ”. Nine of the 159 countries who backed a 2021 Global Methane Pledge reaffirmed their aim to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% by 2030 at the event, which was co-hosted by Brazil, China and the UK. Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Indonesia, Micronesia, Norway, the Netherlands and the UK endorsed this “ ministerial declaration ”, committing to accelerate action towards the 2030 goal.  Separately, Australia endorsed a COP30 statement on reducing methane emissions from fossil-fuel production.  At the beginning of the second week of COP31, Mia Mottley , the prime minister of Barbados, launched a petition calling to “reduc[e] methane emissions to near zero”.  On 11 November, the daily COP31 theme centred on “zero waste”. Emine Erdoğan , the Turkish first lady and chair of a UN advisory board on waste, launched a “ global zero waste alliance ”. This aims to “build a strong foundation for cooperation where countries learn from one another” on cutting waste, said Erdoğan at the launch event. Despite this focus, the Guardian reported before COP31 that Turkey has some of the “world’s worst landfill methane leaks”.  .cb-tweet img{ border: solid 1.25px #333333; border-radius: 5px; } @media (max-width:650px){ .cb-tweet{ width:100%; } } New climate science On day one of COP31, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) presented its State of the Climate 2026 update – the latest in its annual series of reports unpacking key climate indicators. The report finds that 2026 will be one of four warmest years on record. The global average surface temperature for January-September 2026 was about 1.47C above the pre-industrial average, says the report.  It adds that El Niño is forecast to continue into early 2027, further boosting global temperatures . At a press conference to launch the report on 9 November, WMO secretary general Prof Celeste Saulo warned that “this 2026-27 El Niño is off the charts ”, adding that “it is different from any El Niño that we have monitored”.  Saulo warned that “we are supercharging our weather” and that “the human and economic cost is unacceptably high”. She continued: “In 2026, millions of people were exposed to unbearable heat, leading to tens of thousands of excess deaths in Europe alone. India and Pakistan and large parts of Asia and North America suffered dangerous heatwaves. And, as we head into the southern hemisphere summer, we will see more. “The catastrophe in China and Nepal showed the dangers of high-mountain disasters for downstream communities.” She concluded with a call to improve early warning systems, stating that “sustained observations from every part of the world are more important than ever”. The following day, the Global Carbon Project released its latest annual assessment on CO2 emissions and carbon sinks. The 21st edition of the report, written by more than 100 experts from around the world, finds that the world is projected to emit 32.8bn tonnes of CO2 this year, marking a 0.4% decrease compared to 2025. According to the report, CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and cement are set to fall by around 0.4% in 2026, largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz. (This follows separate analysis by Carbon Brief earlier this year suggesting there would be a 0.5% fall due to the Hormuz crisis.) Meanwhile, it finds that emissions from coal are continuing to increase slightly. (For more on the findings, read Carbon Brief’s detailed write-up of the report.) A subset of the report’s authors also published a study in Nature Climate Change on 10 November, stating that “acceleration in clean technology deployment is needed to guarantee emissions peak and subsequent decline”.  Another Nature Climate Change paper , published on the opening day of COP31, finds that regions worldwide may have already experienced around 90-94% of the warming expected when the global average reaches 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.  Food and water A number of initiatives relating to food and water were launched during COP31. “Food security” – including transforming agriculture and focusing on water and drought – was one of the priority themes in the COP31 presidency’s “ action agenda ”. (See: Action agenda .) Despite this, only a few prominent announcements arrived compared to previous years.  On 9 November, when the daily COP theme centred on food, agriculture and health, thinktank Clim-Eat launched a report on the reform of agricultural subsidies. This noted that governments spend approximately $840bn (£638bn) on support and subsidies for agriculture, a sector which majorly contributes to climate change and environmental degradation .  The report outlined ways to move these subsidies towards payments supporting soil health, public infrastructure and increasing farm incomes in a more targeted way.  On 10 November, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) launched a platform aimed at helping countries boost alignment in managing food security, water and climate action, called the “ turquoise nexus initiative “.  Led by Turkey, it will exist within the FAO’s “ food and agriculture for sustainable transformation ” (FAST) partnership, which was launched at COP27 in 2022.  This is designed to boost climate finance for the transformation of food systems, while also supporting efforts on adaptation and other issues.  İbrahim Yumaklı, Turkey’s agriculture minister, said the “turquoise” platform would be used to strengthen existing initiatives, rather than create new ones.  İbrahim Yumaklı, Turkish minister of agriculture, at the launch of the turquoise nexus initiative in Antalya, Turkey on 10 November. Credit: Earth Negotiations Bulletin On 11 November, Ethiopia joined a group of eight other nations in the Alliance of Champions for Food Systems Transformation (ACF), a coalition launched at COP28 in 2023.  This sent a “powerful signal that food systems belong at the heart of climate action”, given that Ethiopia is due to host COP32 next year, said Emma Williams , the head of the ACF secretariat, in a statement . NDCs On 27 October, the UNFCCC released its annual report on nationally determined contributions (NDCs). These documents outline countries’ ambitions, as agreed under the Paris Agreement, to limit greenhouse gas emissions up to 2035. Based on analysis of the latest NDCs, the report says emissions are due to decrease by around 9% by 2035, compared to 2019 levels, if all pledges are implemented – a drop from the 12% reduction estimated in last year’s report . This leaves countries “substantially off track” to limit global temperatures to 1.5C, the report says. A small number of countries announced new NDCs around the time of COP31. Argentina, Botswana, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Egypt, Guatemala, North Macedonia, Palestine and Tajikistan all submitted new pledges in November. Libya also submitted its first-ever NDC, committing to reducing its carbon emissions per unit of its gross domestic product (GDP) by 28% by 2035. Protests and access  Nearly 10,000 people marched through the streets of Antalya on Saturday 14 November, protesting climate change, genocide in Gaza and human-rights abuses in Turkey. “2.8? Unacceptable”Thousands of climate protesters are out on the streets of Antalya right now 🌎 — Daisy Dunne (@daisydunne.carbonbrief.org) 2026-11-14T12:04:26.419Z The middle Saturday of COP is the summit’s traditional “protest day”.  Le Monde reported that Antalya’s protest “stood out for its scale in a country where the space for protest, both environmental and political, is narrow”. Elsewhere at the summit, Swedish campaigner Greta Thunberg made her first appearance at a UN climate summit since COP26 in Glasgow in 2021. Speaking to a huddle of journalists on 12 November, she said: “The climate crisis is already here and now – and it is already a matter of life and death.  “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.” Here’s a video of Greta Thunberg speaking alongside global south activists at COP this morning. More from the speakers, including Mohammad Usrof, Sagar Dhakal, Rikki Dank and Celine Isimbi, on CB Connect: connect.carbonbrief.org/t/greta-thun… — Daisy Dunne (@daisydunne.carbonbrief.org) 2026-11-12T09:58:00.064Z She was joined by global-south campaigners, including Mohammed Usrof , a climate activist and researcher from Gaza, who called out countries that continue to supply fossil fuels to Israel, telling journalists: “Corporations continue to fuel not just genocide in Palestine, but the devastation of the world. [There is a] never-ending proliferation of fossil fuels that we are seeing the consequences all over the global majority world. “So, it’s extremely crucial here to recognise what is happening in this COP, the stakes that we are here for [and] the stakes that our lived realities essentially symbolise to these negotiations.” Other speakers alongside Thunberg included Sagar Dhakal , a young Nepalese politician, who said “there are not any words in the dictionary” to describe the catastrophic flash floods in his country earlier this year, in addition to First Nations activist Rikki Dank and Rwanda-DRC activist Celine Isimbi . COP31 was plagued with logistical problems – particularly during the summit’s opening days – forcing delegates to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to access the venue. The delays sparked serious access concerns, with the ECO newsletter – a daily bulletin put together by campaigners – writing on 11 November: “Participation is not a courtesy the presidency gives out when it’s convenient. It is written into the system. Under Article 4.1(i) of the convention, parties committed to encourage ‘the widest participation’ in this process, including by non-governmental organisations. Article 12 of the Paris Agreement calls for public participation and public access to information. Nobody added a footnote saying ‘subject to traffic conditions’.” During the first part of the final plenary on 20 November, a protester – who was wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” – was ejected after standing on a chair with a red noose around their neck. Road to COP32 and beyond At COP30 , it was agreed that COP32 in 2027 will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Under the UN’s regional rotational system for hosting COP, the country will be representing the African region . It will be the first-ever COP hosted by one of the least-developed countries . Ethiopia’s prime minister Abiy Ahmed addressed the world leaders’ summit at COP31, touting his country’s fossil fuel-free electricity grid and pledging to make finance for developing countries a central part of COP32. He told other leaders:  “Dependable finance requires cooperation, even as competition between countries grows. Yet, we discuss climate in one room, development in another, trade and finance in two more. Many of us see it in all four. In each of those rooms we should ask how we will finance the future that we have agreed to build.” (There have been some concerns that conflict in the country might affect its ability to host.) During the first week of COP31, China ruled out hosting COP33 in 2028, which is due to be held in Asia. (In August, Bloomberg reported that the world’s largest emitter was considering hosting the conference.) India had withdrawn a bid to host COP33 in April. Countries that are considering making a bid to host COP33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand, according to the Guardian . In the table below, Carbon Brief has compiled key meetings and milestones leading up to COP32 in Ethiopia. 11-22 January Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction COP1 , New York  May Second transitioning away from fossil fuels pre-conference , Dublin, Ireland  7-17 June Bonn climate talks , Germany 19-27 June London climate action week July Second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference , Tuvalu 8-22 September UN general assembly , New York 19-26 September New York climate week 8-19 November COP32 , Addis Ababa, Ethiopia Edited by Dr Simon Evans, Leo Hickman and Molly Lempriere. title: The World’s Biggest Climate Conference Just Fell Apart
zh_title: 世界上最大的气候会议刚刚破裂
summary: 如果不出意外的话，联合国年度气候会议可以让世界领导人将注意力集中在地球命运上一两周。不过，在今年的会议期间，特朗普总统、习近平主席和普京总统在中国会面，同意增加石油产量；只有一位七国集团领导人，即英国首相安迪·伯纳姆，出现在土耳其安塔利亚举行的联合国会议（即第 31 届缔约方大会）上。当一位世界领导人确实出现在会议上时，媒体就会聚集在一起，马雷克·普鲁谢维奇 (Marek Pruszewicz) 是英国广播公司 (BBC) 的前编辑。
content:
如果不出意外的话，联合国年度气候会议可以让世界领导人将注意力集中在地球命运上一两周。不过，在今年的会议期间，特朗普总统、习近平主席和普京总统在中国会面，同意增加石油产量；只有一位七国集团领导人，即英国首相安迪·伯纳姆，出现在土耳其安塔利亚举行的联合国会议（即第 31 届缔约方大会）上。英国广播公司 (BBC) 前编辑马雷克·普鲁谢维奇 (Marek Pruszewicz) 告诉我，当世界领导人确实出席会议时，媒体就会蜂拥而至，他现在负责气候出版物《对话地球》。但当领导人离开后，记者们似乎也同样消失得无影无踪。他看到电视记者在空座位和一排排空置的记者席上工作。 “它只是没有突破，”普鲁谢维奇说。美国今年最大的气候斗争也是如此，这场斗争是围绕参议院周四通过的一项许可改革法案进行的。支持者认为，该法案对于清洁能源的蓬勃发展是必要的；反对者将其视为给天然气公司的礼物。如果你与参与这场辩论的人交谈，或者深入研究正在大声争论这些问题的社交媒体角落，你仍然会发现关于地球命运的激烈争论。但很难摆脱这样一种感觉：世界似乎不像以前那样关心解决这个问题了。
周日，COP 谈判在该会议 30 年历史上第三次破裂。世界各国外交官在这些气候谈判中花费了 20 多年时间，才同意提及化石燃料（全球变暖的主要驱动因素）作为问题的一部分。这种情况发生在五年前，在格拉斯哥举行的联合国气候峰会上，当时谈判代表们同意的不是“逐步淘汰”，而是“逐步减少”煤炭的使用。第二年，在埃及沙姆沙伊赫，数十个国家敦促达成协议，“逐步减少”所有化石燃料；直到 2023 年，在迪拜，外交官们才承诺提出“过渡”这一更为热烈的想法。过去两周在安塔利亚举行的谈判使过去的努力听起来雄心勃勃，甚至是理想化的。在本周的谈判中，谈判代表从协议草案中删除了所有涉及化石燃料以及减少世界对化石燃料依赖的内容。谈判代表还不再提及发达国家对造成气候变化的历史责任。气候倡导组织“非洲权力转移”主任穆罕默德·阿多周五对记者表示，这是“有史以来最糟糕的一次缔约方大会”。谈判陷入加时，谈判代表试图达成一项能够获得通过的必要共识的协议，但周日，他们承认失败了。
主办国在会议开始时制定的签名提案是设定一个目标，即到 2035 年将世界能源消耗中电气化的比例从目前的 23% 提高到 35%。这一转变被认为对于最终降低碳排放非常重要，通过用电动替代品取代内燃机汽车和燃油加热器，即使它们的电力来自燃烧化石燃料的发电厂，电动替代品也可以更加高效。达到“35 x 35”并不容易——这需要将电气化的步伐加快四倍以上——但实现这一目标仍然无法保持气氛

【原文 English Original】
If for nothing else, the United Nations’ annual climate gathering can be useful for focusing world leaders’ attention on the fate of the planet for a week or two. During this year’s conference, though, Presidents Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin were instead meeting with one another in China, where they agreed to increase oil production; only one G7 leader, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, showed up in Antalya, Turkey, where the UN conference, known as COP 31, was held. When a world leader did appear at the conference, a media scrum would form, Marek Pruszewicz, a former BBC editor who now runs the climate publication Dialogue Earth , told me. But when the leaders left, reporters seemed to vanish just as quickly. He saw television journalists working amid empty seats and rows of vacant press tables. “It’s just not cutting through,” Pruszewicz said. The same could be said of the year’s biggest climate fight in the United States, over a permitting-reform bill that the Senate passed on Thursday. Proponents argue that the bill is necessary for clean energy to thrive; opponents see it as a gift to gas companies. If you talk with people involved in this debate, or dip into the corners of social media where the issues are being litigated out loud, you’ll still find vehement arguments about the fate of the planet. But it’s hard to shake the feeling that the world seems to care less about solving this problem than it once did. On Sunday, the COP negotiations collapsed for only the third time in the conference’s 30-year history. The world’s diplomats spent more than 20 years at these climate negotiations before they agreed to even mention fossil fuels, the dominant driver of global warming, as part of the problem. That happened five years ago, at the UN climate summit in Glasgow, when negotiators agreed not on a “phase out” but on just a “phase down” of the use of coal. The following year, in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, dozens of countries pressed for an agreement to “phase down” all fossil fuels; only in 2023, in Dubai, did diplomats commit to the more effervescent idea of a “transitioning away.” The negotiations over the past two weeks in Antalya made those past efforts sound ambitious, even idealistic. During the talks this week, negotiators stripped out all references to fossil fuels and to reducing the world’s dependence on them from a draft agreement. The negotiators also cut references to the historical responsibility of developed countries for causing climate change. Mohamed Adow, the director of Power Shift Africa, a climate-advocacy group, told reporters on Friday that this has been “the worst COP ever.” The negotiations ran into overtime, as negotiators tried to land on an agreement that could gain the necessary consensus to pass, but on Sunday, they admitted that they had failed. The signature proposal, set by the host nation at the conference’s outset, was to set a goal of increasing the proportion of electrification of the world’s energy consumption from 23 percent, where it is now, to 35 percent by 2035. This shift is seen as important for eventually lowering carbon emissions, by switching out internal-combustion cars and oil heaters with electric alternatives, which can be more efficient even if their electricity comes from power plants burning fossil fuels. Reaching “35 by 35” would not be easy—it would require a more than fourfold speedup in the pace of electrification—but hitting that goal still wouldn’t keep the atmosphere from warming 2 or more degrees Celsius from the baseline before the Industrial Revolution. That amounts to “catastrophic global warming,” Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, told me from Antalya last week. The electrification goal, he said, was, to begin with, a “minor and insufficient consolation.” Ultimately, the negotiations broke down in part over the question of whether the agreement would mention fossil fuels at all. Some environmentalists worry that Congress, too, is too willing to ignore the problem of fossil fuels’ future. The bipartisan permitting bill, which will now head to the House, would rewrite bedrock environmental laws to speed up the build-out of transmission lines and new sources of clean energy. But these laws would also make it easier to build all sorts of infrastructure, including (opponents point out) gas pipelines, data centers, and ICE-detention centers, as well as (proponents note) ecological-restoration projects. Like COP’s organizers, the architects of this bill see it as a practical measure that will continue advancing climate goals. One of its sponsors is Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, who has been one of the most consistent advocates for climate policy in Congress. The bill’s supporters argue that it clears the way for clean energy to continue its takeover, even if, in the short term, the bill also helps the fossil-fuel industry. (Opponents see fossil-fuel companies as better positioned to take advantage of any new build-out.) Some former Biden-administration staffers believe that the bill could fix a problem they ran into with their signature climate legislation: They made it easier to build solar and wind farms, but not easier to build the power lines to connect them to anything. No one thinks that the bill does enough, on its own, to dramatically change the trajectory of U.S. emissions; people on both sides of the argument fear a future in which the status quo sticks. Climate scientists are taking encouragement where they can. If the biggest climate fights of 2027 will be focused on limited “practical” questions, then so will the clearest advances: The use of solar- and other renewable-energy sources is growing. So is the adoption of EVs. Both are happening far faster in many other countries than they are in the United States. Still, the reminders about the costs of continued warming were hard to miss this year: the glacier collapse in Nepal that swept away more than 1,500 people. The summer heat wave in Europe that killed some 50,000 more. The El Niño in an already overheated Pacific Ocean that’s spinning out droughts and floods around the world. Climate scientists say the goal of keeping warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius will inevitably be surpassed; the latest report by the World Meteorological Organization found that global mean temperatures from January to September were 1.47 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels. Celeste Saulo, the WMO secretary general, told reporters last week that the past dozen years have been the warmest on record, and the past four, including 2026, were the warmest of those. “There is no end in sight,” she said. The question has moved to how bad the “overshoot” period will be and what can be done to minimize the damage and avoid tipping points. “That includes your large ice sheets melting, glaciers melting,” Rachel Cleetus, the climate-program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, told me. “Once that happens, you can’t bring them back.” The mood going into COP was “pretty somber,” she said, in a year when climate disasters have piled up and fossil-fuel companies reported record profits. She had left for Antalya from Boston amid fall temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit. By the time the COP talks ended with little to show, most everyone had gone home, and the mood was grim.

title: Alleged UK spy for Hong Kong died by suicide ahead of trial, British jury rules
zh_title: 英国陪审团裁定，被指控为香港的英国间谍在审判前自杀身亡
summary: 英国陪审团发现，一名被指控为香港从事间谍活动的前英国海军陆战队员自杀身亡。马修·特里克特（Matthew Trickett）在一家公共服务公司未能找到他并安装他的电子标签后结束了自己的生命。马修·特里克特（Matthew Trickett）是被伦敦警方指控涉嫌为香港从事间谍活动的三名男子之一。照片：皇家海军陆战队。 2024 年 5 月，这位 37 岁的男子被发现死于梅登黑德的格伦费尔公园。几周前，他因涉嫌协助香港情报部门而根据英国国家安全法被捕并受到指控。 Trickett – 内政部移民办公室
content:
英国陪审团发现，一名被指控为香港从事间谍活动的前英国海军陆战队员自杀身亡。马修·特里克特（Matthew Trickett）在一家公共服务公司未能找到他并安装他的电子标签后结束了自己的生命。马修·特里克特（Matthew Trickett）是被伦敦警方指控涉嫌为香港从事间谍活动的三名男子之一。照片：皇家海军陆战队。 2024 年 5 月，这位 37 岁的男子被发现死于梅登黑德的格伦费尔公园。几周前，他因涉嫌协助香港情报部门而根据英国国家安全法被捕并受到指控。特里克特是内政部移民官员，在拘留期间被发现在牢房内试图自残，但两天后被保释。 💡 如果您需要支援，请致电：撒玛利亚会 2896 0000（24小时，多语种）、预防自杀中心 2382 0000 或政府心理健康热线 18111。香港辅导及心理学会提供中英文 WhatsApp 热线：6218 1084。另请参阅：HKFP 心理健康热线卫生服务指南。据英国广播公司报道，雷丁验尸官法院的陪审团周三发现，为英国政府提供司法和惩教服务的 Serco 多次“未能采取合理措施”找到他的地址。特里克特的同案被告卫彼得·韦(Peter Wai)和袁国强(Bill Yuen)因协助香港外国情报部门于6月分别被判入狱10年和8年。
前英国边防部队官员韦伟被判在香港驻伦敦经济贸易办事处办事处经理袁先生的命令下进行“影子警务”行动。左起：香港经济贸易办事处（香港经贸办）官员袁国强和前英国边防部队官员韦伟伟。照片：伦敦警察厅。这两名具有中英双重国籍的人针对的是居住在英国的香港民主抗议者。香港否认与明显的间谍活动有任何联系。全文：解释者：英国当局为何逮捕与香港驻伦敦经济贸易办事处（香港经济贸易办事处）有联系的 3 名男子。照片：维基共享资源。据称，这两人监视的人中有活动人士罗冠聪 (Nathan Law)，他被香港国安警察通缉，悬赏 100 万港元。由于担心“羞辱”，特里克特于 2024 年 5 月 23 日（即他应出庭的前一天）写了一封给家人的最后一封信。据报道，陪审团表示：“在得知警方试图找到他并担心他会被逮捕并重新拘留后，马特提前了他的计划，并将信函的日期重新调整为 5 月 19 日。”特里克特的一位朋友上周告诉法庭，特里克特自 2013 年以来一直担任私人安全顾问，他担心可能的定罪会带来“耻辱”，并警告他可能会自杀。马修·特里克特（Matthew Trickett）是被伦敦警方指控涉嫌为香港从事间谍活动的三名男子之一。
照片：LinkedIn via M.Trickett 高级验尸官 Heidi Connor 表示 Serco 尚未进行内部调查，并补充说该公司必须“改进其系统”以降低更多人死亡的风险。一个简单的谷歌地图搜索就可以避免她所说的“非常罕见”的情况。在周三的裁决之后，Serco 的发言人表示，该公司将审查验尸官的报告和建议。

【原文 English Original】
A former British marine who was charged with spying for Hong Kong died by suicide, a UK jury has found. Matthew Trickett took his own life after a public services firm failed to locate him and fit his electronic tag. Matthew Trickett, one of the three men charged by London police on suspicion of spying for Hong Kong. Photo: Royal Marines. In May 2024, the 37-year-old was found dead in Maidenhead’s Grenfell Park. He had been arrested and charged under the UK’s National Security Act weeks earlier for allegedly assisting Hong Kong’s intelligence service. Trickett – a Home Office immigration officer – was seen attempting self-harm in his cell while in detention, but was released on bail two days later. 💡 If you are in need of support , please call: The Samaritans 2896 0000 (24-hour, multilingual), Suicide Prevention Centre 2382 0000 or the gov’ t mental health hotline on 18111. The Hong Kong Society of Counselling and Psychology provides a WhatsApp hotline in English and Chinese: 6218 1084. See also: HKFP’s mental health services guide. On multiple occasions, Serco – which provides judicial and correctional services to the UK government – “failed to take reasonable steps” to locate his address, the jury at Reading Coroner’s Court found on Wednesday, according to the BBC. Peter Wai and Bill Yuen, Trickett’s co-defendants, were jailed for 10 and eight years, respectively, in June for assisting Hong Kong’s foreign intelligence service. Wai, a former UK Border Force officer, was convicted of conducting a “shadow policing” operation upon the orders of Yuen, an office manager at the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in London. From left: Hong Kong Economic Trade Office (HKETO) official Bill Yuen and former UK Border Force officer Peter Wai. Photos: Metropolitan Police. The two British-Chinese dual nationals targeted Hong Kong pro-democracy protesters living in the UK. Hong Kong denied any link to the apparent spying . In full: Explainer: Why UK authorities arrested 3 men linked to Hong Kong’s trade office The Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office (HKETO) in London. Photo: Wikimedia Commons. Among those the pair were said to have surveilled was activist Nathan Law, who is wanted by national security police in Hong Kong with a HK$1 million bounty on his head. Fear of ‘humiliation’ Trickett had penned a final letter to his family dated May 23, 2024 – the day before he was due to appear in court. “Upon learning that police were trying to locate him and fearing he would be arrested and taken back to custody, Matt brought his plan forward and re-dated his letter to May 19,” the jury reportedly said. One of his friends told the court last week that Trickett, who had worked as a private security consultant since 2013, feared the “humiliation” of a possible conviction and had warned he might kill himself. Matthew Trickett, one of the three men charged by London police on suspicion of spying for Hong Kong. Photo: LinkedIn via M. Trickett Senior coroner Heidi Connor said Serco had yet to carry out an internal investigation, adding that the company must “improve its systems” to mitigate the risk of more people dying. A simple Google Maps search could have averted what she nevertheless said was a “very rare” scenario. Following Wednesday’s ruling, a spokesperson for Serco said the company would review the coroner’s report and recommendation.

title: Populists vs. Protesters: Czechs Fight Over Public Broadcasters

content:
一年中的大部分时间里，莱特纳平原都没有什么可以为当地人或游客提供的东西。这是布拉格斯巴达足球场对面的一大片毫无特色的土地。表面交替出现灰尘和泥土；有一个巴士停车场，有时还有马戏团。但莱特纳偶尔会举办一些可以让捷克政坛发生倾斜的活动。有时有一点。有时很多。 1989 年 11 月 25 日星期六，大约 75 万人聚集在一起，要求结束捷克斯洛伐克的共产主义政权。第二天，许多人返回，并于 11 月 29 日星期三，议会废除了共产党在社会中的领导地位。这次不会再发生类似的事情，但 11 月 15 日星期日，莱特纳岛上大约有 40 万人参加了自天鹅绒革命以来布拉格最大规模的示威活动。从媒体平台上俯瞰旗帜和面孔的海洋时，它看起来很大。数万人聚集在那里抗议政府计划取消每月 10 美元的许可费，该许可费为该国两家公共广播公司捷克电视台和捷克广播电台提供资金。这似乎不是一个令人愤慨的提议，但对许多捷克人来说，这加深了他们对亿万富翁总理安德烈·巴比什及其民粹主义联盟的不信任。这位总理多年来一直在法庭上与欧盟补贴欺诈指控作斗争，他不喜欢公共广播。

For much of the year, Letná Plain has nothing to offer either locals or tourists.  It’s a large, featureless patch of land opposite the Sparta Prague football stadium. The surface alternates between dust and mud; there’s a car park for buses, and sometimes a circus. But every so often, Letná hosts an event that can tilt the world of Czech politics on its axis. Sometimes a little. Sometimes a lot.  On Saturday, November 25, 1989, around 750,000 people gathered to demand the end of Czechoslovakia’s communist regime. The following day, many returned, and on Wednesday, November 29, parliament abolished the Communist Party’s leading role in society. Nothing like that is going to happen this time around, but on Sunday, November 15, there were perhaps 400,000 people on Letná for the largest demonstration in Prague since the Velvet Revolution. It looked huge when viewed from a media platform overlooking an ocean of flags and faces.   The people who had gathered in the tens of thousands were there to protest against government plans to scrap the $10 monthly license fee which funds the nation’s two public broadcasters, Czech TV and Czech Radio. This may not seem an outrageous proposal, but to many Czechs it deepens their distrust of their billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babiš and his populist coalition.   The premier, who has spent years in court fighting EU subsidy fraud allegations , is no fan of public broadcasting.  Get the Latest Sign up to receive regular emails and stay informed about CEPA's work. In 2017, Babiš, who was then finance minister, described Czech TV’s investigative reporters as “a corrupt rabble making reports to order.” In 2024, he said public broadcasters were part of the then governing coalition’s “media division.”  But it is his coalition ally, the far-right SPD party, that has spearheaded the campaign to scrap the license fees and replace them with direct state funding. The fear is that state funds will come with strings pulled by politicians. Tokyo-born businessman Tomio Okamura, the SPD chairman and now parliament’s speaker, has said he would vote for a bill to abolish the broadcasters altogether if someone submitted one.  The third coalition partner is the MAGA-friendly Motorists for Themselves party, which was against scrapping the fees but is now in favor. One Motorist MP said public broadcasting had been turned into a totem by one half of Czech society, which was giving the other half the finger.  What is clear is that the government has not covered itself in glory. After months of vague and occasionally rancorous debate, and just days after all three coalition parties did poorly in Senate and local elections, the first reading of the bill was rushed through parliament in the middle of the night, with a vote scheduled for 4:36 am on Saturday, October 24. The bill envisages a cut in funding of around 15%, reversing an increase introduced by the previous government. Babiš is also floating alternative funding mechanisms, including voluntary contributions, and insists the government will not interfere in editorial decisions.  But there is a glaring contradiction. His government’s own impact assessment identifies the license fee as the funding mechanism that carries the smallest risk to the broadcasters’ independence. Direct state funding, it says, carries the greatest risk.  There has been much talk of “the Nordic model,” without acknowledging that there is no single Nordic model. Finland and Sweden, for example, have dedicated levies collected through the tax system, but Babiš has ruled out a new tax.  Observers are more worried about “the Slovak model.” There, the license fee was abolished in 2023 with a solemn promise to ringfence funding for Slovak Radio and TV and preserve its independence.  The following year, the broadcaster was dissolved by Robert Fico’s populist nationalist government and replaced. Critics say its successor is now toeing the government line. Babiš said he would not be deterred by mass demonstrations, though there was a tiny wobble from Culture Minister Oto Klempíř, who said after talks with Michael McGrath, the European Commissioner for Democracy and Justice, that he wanted to delay further debate on the bill until parliament had begun discussing legislation to implement the European Media Freedom Act.  The 72-year-old prime minister is in a tough spot. He seems tired and barely invested in the issue while his far-right coalition partner insists the fee has to go. Babiš is known to dislike big demonstrations, and the opposition senses an opportunity.  Following Klempíř’s suggestion to kick the issue into the long grass would be a logical course of action for the prime minister, but it may not be one that’s open to him.  Rob Cameron is a Prague-based journalist and broadcaster, and author of https://www.basedinbohemia.com/ where he writes about Central Europe through reporting, analysis and long-form storytelling. He spent 22 years as the BBC’s correspondent in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, covering politics, business, culture and major breaking news across radio, television and online. He is a regular contributor to a number of international broadcasters, including Deutsche Welle, RTÉ and Monocle Radio. He has lived in Prague since 1993 and has reported extensively across Central and Eastern Europe.   Europe’s Edge  is CEPA’s online journal covering critical topics on the foreign policy docket across Europe and North America.
